# 7. [SAA] EC2 Placement Groups
# Section: EC2 for CloudOps
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512508
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about placement groups.
Placement groups are a little bit more advanced,
and we wanna use them once,
we want to have control over how our EC2 instances
are going to be placed within the AWS infrastructure.
So that strategy can be defined
using these placement groups.
So we don't get direct interaction with the hardware of AWS,
but we let AWS know how we would like our EC2 instance
to be placed compared to one another.
So when you create a placement group,
you have three strategies available for you.
You have the cluster placement group in which your instances
will be grouped together in a low-latency hardware setup
within a single availability zone.
This is going to give you high performance but high risk.
We'll see this in details in a second.
Spread means that your instances
are going to be spread across different hardware,
and there is a restriction on this.
That means you can only have seven EC2 instance
per placement group that spread per AZ.
So you would use a spread placement group
when you have critical applications.
Finally, the last one is a new kind
of placement group that is really helpful.
It's called partition.
It's similar to the spread,
meaning that you want to spread your instances,
but here, they're spread across many different partitions.
And these partitions rely on different sets of racks
of hardware within an AZ.
What does that mean is that they're still spread,
but they're not isolated one from another failure,
but a partition should be isolated
from another partition of failure.
The idea with this is that you can scale to hundreds
of EC2 instances per group, and that allows you
to run applications such as Hadoop,
Cassandra, or Kafka.
Now, let's have a look into each
of these placement groups in details.
So next, we have the cluster placement group,
and all your EC2 instances are going to be
in the same availability zone.
So why do we do this?
Well, this particular placement group
gives you great networking.
So you have around 10 gigabits per second
of bandwidth between all these instances
that will have enhanced networking enabled.
And so you get low latency, high throughput network.
And the idea is that out of this,
you can get great performance
for any kind of computational job.
So a drawback of using this architecture
is that if your availability zone fails,
then all the instances will fail at the same time.
But usually, for use case, this is fine.
So the use cases for this kind of placement group
are big data jobs that need to complete very fast
with very high networking
or applications that need extremely low latency
and high throughput network
between each instance of your application.
Now, spread is the complete opposite.
In spread, we want to minimize the failure risk.
And so in this case, when we ask for spread placement group,
all the EC2 instances are going to be located
on different hardware.
So as you can see here, we have three AZ,
and we have six EC2, and each EC2 instance
is on a different hardware.
So what does that mean?
Well, what we get is that we can span across multiple AZ,
and there is a reduced risk of simultaneous failure.
Why?
Well, because if my hardware one fails,
I'm pretty sure my hardware two will not fail.
And so we've separated the risk
of my two instances in the Us-east-1a
to fail at the same time.
And so that's the benefit from it.
The con is that from this configuration,
we're limited to seven instances per AZ per placement group.
So there is a limit to how big your placement group can be.
And so you need to have application
that's gonna be of good size but not too big.
The use case would be an application that needs to maximize
high availability and reduce the risk.
And in general, for critical applications
where your instance failures must be isolated
from one another.
Remember, here, we have a limitation
of seven instances per AZ per placement group.
Now, for the partition placement group,
we can have instances spread across partitions
in multiple available T-zones.
So we can have up to seven partitions per AZ.
So in this example, we have partition one
and partition two in us-east-1a
and partition three in us-east-1b.
And on each partition, you can have many EC2 instances.
So in the first one have four,
and the second one have four,
and the third one have four as well.
So why do we use a partition placement group?
Well, each partition represents a rack in AWS.
And so by having many partitions, you're making sure
that your instances are distributed
across many hardware racks, and so therefore,
they're safe from a rack failure from one another.
So you can have up to seven partitions per AZ,
and these partitions can span
across multiple availability zones in the same region.
You can get up to hundreds of EC2 instances with the setup.
So this is a difference
versus the spread type of placement group.
And as I said, the instances in the partition
do not share the same hardware physical rack
with the instances in the other partitions,
and therefore, each partition is isolated from failure.
So that means that, yes, if one goes down,
if partition goes down, the partition number two,
then partition number one should be fine.
And to know which partition these EC2 instances are on,
there is an option to access this information
with using the metadata service.
So when would you use a partition placement group?
Well, when you have an application
that it can be partition aware to distribute the data
and your servers across partitions.
And usually, the use cases
are going to be big data applications
which are partition aware, such as using HDFS,
HBase, Cassandra, and Apache Kafka.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

Instance Connect feature.

# 14. EC2 Instance Status Checks
# Section: EC2 for CloudOps
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512590
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's have a look at status checks.
So status checks on your EC2 instances are automated checks
done by AWS for you that will identify hardware
and software issues with your EC2 instances.
So the first type is a system status check,
and this will be a monitoring of problems that will happen
with the systems of AWS directly, for example, a software
or a hardware issue on the actual physical host
that will be used, that will be the one
that your EC2 instance is placed on.
Or for example, if your host has a loss of system power
and so on.
To have a overview of these issues,
a place to look at is the Personal Health Dashboard
and this will give you an information
around any scheduled critical maintenance by AWS
that will affect, that will, sorry,
affect your EC2 instance host
and therefore you need to act on it.
So a way to act on it is to stop and start your instance.
So let's have a look.
As we can see here, we have a host one,
this is hidden to us, okay?
But this is what happens in the data center of AWS,
and our EC2 instance is launched onto this host one.
Then say that AWS has a hardware failure,
then this system status check will be going from zero
to one, and what we have to do is to stop
and start the EC2 instance.
So anytime you stop an EC2 instance
and then you start it again.
So not a reboot, right? But a stop and a start.
Then internally what's going to happen
is that your EC2 instance will automatically be migrated
to a different host within AWS,
which also explains
why it will get a new difference public IP,
because this will be the public IP
of the host you're on.
Okay? So this is a different host migration.
So it goes from host one to host two,
and because what we'll just stopped and started,
then we know that it's moved
and the host two does not have any issues
and so therefore we have solved
our hardware failure problem.
The second type of problem is an instance status check.
This is to monitor software
and network configuration of your instance.
For example, the network configuration becomes invalid.
There's exhausted memory, this kind of stuff,
in which case to just resolve this issue,
you should just reboot the EC2 instance
or change the instance configuration.
Finally, there is a new status check
called the attached EBS status check, which is going
to monitor the EBS volumes attached to your instance
to see if they are reachable
and to see if they can complete IO operations.
And in case you have an issue with your EBS volumes,
then you should reboot the instance
or replace the affected EBS volumes.
So that's it for the three status checks.
But there is a way for you to automate the recovery
and look at CloudWatch Metrics, so.
CloudWatch metrics are status check failed system,
status check failed instance,
and status check failed attached EBS,
or if you have any of these issue,
you also have status check failed,
which groups the three together.
So option one is to use CloudWatch Alarm
to recover your EC2 instance.
So there is an action called recover instance.
And when it's being used by CloudWatch Alarm,
it will recover the instance by using the same private IP,
the same public IP, the same EIP,
the same metadata and same placement group.
You can also send a notification
because it's a CloudWatch Alarm, directly to SNS.
So your EC2 instance will be monitored
by CloudWatch Metrics, for example,
for the status checked failed system metric.
The CloudWatch alarm will be triggered on top
of your CloudWatch Metric in case it goes to one,
and the action of your CloudWatch alarm will be
to recover your EC2 instance by placing it somewhere else.
You can also send an notification to Amazon SNS,
as I just said.
The option two, which is a bit more less con,
a bit less conventional, is to use an auto scaling group
with a min, max and desired of one
and with an health check to check for the status check
of your EC2 instance.
What will happen is that in case there is a issue
with your EC2 instance, it will be terminated
by your auto scaling group,
and therefore because we have a min, max
and desire to one, a new EC2 instance will be launched
within your same auto scaling group.
So in this case, you don't have the same EBS volumes,
you don't have the same private IP,
you don't have the same elastic IP,
but at least your instance is back up and running.
And if you automate things well,
then you could maybe regain back its state.
Okay? So these are two options.
Obviously, option one is going to be much preferred
if you have emphasis on one specific EC2 instance.
So that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 16. [SAA] EC2 Hibernate
# Section: EC2 for CloudOps
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512600
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about a lesser-known feature
called EC2 Hibernate.
So we know that we can stop and terminate instances,
and when we do so, when we stop it,
the data on disk, on your EBS disk,
is going to be kept intact until the next start.
That makes sense.
And if we terminate it, well,
if you set up the root volume
to be destroyed with your instance,
it's going to be destroyed,
but any volume that is not set up to be destroyed
when your instance is terminated will be kept.
And then when you start an instance,
well, the OS, the operating system will boot
and then the EC2 User Data that was going to be run,
the script, and then the OS will boot up.
And then your application starts, your caches get warmed,
and that can take time,
because you are booting your machine, right?
But the idea is that with Hibernate,
we want to achieve a new state.
So when we hibernate an instance, whatever was in RAM,
the in-memory state is going to be preserved.
What does that mean?
That means that your instance boot is going
to be much faster,
because the operating system is not stopped or restarted,
the operating system is actually just frozen,
it's hibernated.
And under the hood, well,
whatever was in the RAM state is going to be written
into a file in the root EBS volume.
So that means that the root EBS volume must be encrypted
and that it must have enough space to contain the RAM.
So let me show you what happens.
So we take an EC2 instance,
and it's running and there is data in RAM,
and then we start a hibernation process.
So what happens that the instance will go
in the stopping state,
and the RAM is going to be dumped into your EBS volume.
Then the instance is shut down and the RAM disappears,
because as soon as you stop an instance the RAM goes away,
but the EBS volume still contains the dump of the RAM.
And then when your instance is started,
then the RAM is going to be loaded from disk
onto the EC2 instance memory.
And that means that it is just as is
your EC2 instance never got stopped.
And we'll have a look at this in the hands-on.
So the use cases for hibernation is
if you want to have long-running processes
and never actually stop them,
or if you want to save the RAM state,
or if you just want to reboot, like boot up fast,
and you have services that take time to initialize.
So you actually don't want them to initialize,
you want them to stay up and running
even if you hibernate your instance.
So, some good things to know about EC2 Hibernate is that
it supports a lot of different families.
The instance RAM size must be less than 150 gigabytes.
Now, that can change,
and again, you're not tested on limits at the exam,
but I'm just putting this as an indication for you
to get an idea of how that works.
It doesn't work for bare metal instances.
It works for many different operating systems,
including Linux and Windows.
It works for the root volume,
so the root volume must be an EBS volume,
it must be encrypted, okay?
And it must be large to contain the RAM
that you dump onto it.
It's available for all kind of instances,
such as on-demand, reserved, and spot instances.
And hibernation is meant to be no more than 60 days.
Again, this can change,
but right now this is the actual limits.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture for a hands-on.

# 22. AMI No Reboot Option
# Section: AMI - Amazon Machine Image
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512724
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's have a look at one specific option when
creating AMI, which is a No-Reboot option.
So it allows you to create an AMI without first
shutting down your EC2 instance.
And by default it's not selected,
that means that any time we want to create an AMI
we want to shut down the instance before creating the AMI
and this is to maintain the file system integrity.
So this is what happens.
So with the No-Reboot disabled,
if we want to initiate creating an AMI,
the instance is first shut shutdown.
Then after shutdown,
the attached EBS volume will get
a snapshot taken into an EBS snapshot.
And then the EBS snapshot will be converted into an AMI.
Now if you enable the No-Reboot option,
then your EC2 instance that is currently running,
will get a snapshot directly made
onto its running attached EBS volume
and then the image will be created.
So the risk here is to not have a file system integrity.
Also, any OS operating system buffer will not be flushed to
the disc before the snapshot is created.
So you need to make sure that you know what you're doing
when you're creating an AMI
while the instance is still running.
Now, why do I say this?
Well, because when you use the backup service in AWS,
you can create a backup plan
and this allows you to create an AMI.
Now, the backup service does not reboot the instances while
taking EBS snapshot,
so by default, the only option actually
is to have the no-reboot behavior.
That means that when you use AWS backup on Amazon EC2,
the AMIs will be created using the parameter
no-reboots that the instances are not being interrupted
while they're functioning.
So that means that when you use the backup plans,
this will not help you guarantee that the file system will
have its integrity, okay?
Because you will need to reboot the instance first.
And so, as an alternative,
if you wanted to have a scheduled backup of your Amazon
EC2 instance into an AMI,
you could create an EventBridge rule.
So for example, you could create a schedule
which will invoke the Lambda function once every week.
The Lambda function will have its own code to create an AMI,
okay, create an image,
with this time with the reboot option.
In this case, then the Amazon EC2
will be rebooting and an AMI will be created.
So if you have a running instance and you want to see
the option, very simple, right click
and then you do Image and templates, Create Image.
So just like before and in here,
you have no reboot enabled.
And this allows you for your instance to have it snapshot
taken without an AMI being created
without it rebooting first.
So you need to use it at your own risk.
And this is the option that is used by default
when using the backup service.
That's all I wanted to show you in this lecture.
So I can just go ahead and cancel my window.
So that's it.
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 26. AMI In Production
# Section: AMI - Amazon Machine Image
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512790
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay. So just a short theory lecture
on how to use AMIs in production.
So there's a way for you to force users to only launch EC2
instances from pre-approved AMIs,
and what is a pre-approved AMI? Well,
it's an AMI that you're going to tag with a specific tag.
And then when you combine this with an IAM policy,
then you restrict the user to only launch, for example,
AMIs that have been tagged with the environment prod.
So as an example,
we have a user with the appropriate IAM permissions,
as you can see, it's a condition that we apply to the user.
And so now we have two types of AMI within our accounts.
We have the not approved the AMI, the non-approved AMI,
which is the ones that don't have tags.
And the AMI has been approved,
has been correctly tagged for environment prods.
Obviously you need to make sure that
you're also logged down,
who can add tags to your AMIs.
But then thanks to this combination of tags and IAM policy,
while the user is not going to be able to launch EC2
instance from a not approved AMI and is going to be allowed
to launch an AMI from an approved, EC2 instance sorry,
from an approved AMI.
And that's for number one.
So this is to prevent AMIs from being launched
if they're not approved.
But the second thing is that you can have AWS Config to find
non-compliant EC2 instances,
which are EC2 instances that have been launched using
AMIs that were not approved before.
So let's take an example, somehow a user managed to find a
way to launch two EC2 instances,
one from an approved AMI.
And one from one that wasn't approved.
In this case, using config we can write a rule
and it's going to monitor all the EC2 instances
and find if these two EC2 instances are complaint or not.
And the ones are not compliant will be flagged by config,
and then we can take actions.
And the ones are compliant will be marked green.
And we're good to go.
So that's a short theory lecture,
but it's a good way to see how you can have a production
ready set up for your AMIs.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 33. SSM Automations - Patch AMI & Update ASG
# Section: Managing EC2 at Scale - Systems Manager (SSM)
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53218461
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so here is a real-life example
of what an SSM automation may look like.
So for example, say we have an auto-scaling group
and it's running a source AMI,
but we want to actually patch that AMI
and have the auto-scaling group launch EC2 instances
based on a new patched AMI.
So to do so, we must, and we can use an automation
because everything will be managed by AWS.
So what are the steps of our automation?
Well, step number one, we need
to make sure it has a proper IAM role to perform all needs
to do, but then what happens?
We set up the automation,
first of all to launch an EC2 instance
from the source AMI.
And then the second step of the automation is
to do a run command from SSM to install the patches
on your EC2 instance called AWS run patch baseline.
This is going to give you an EC2 instance.
Then you can, that is patched of course, then we can stop it
and when it's stopped, we can create an image.
So again, all these steps are run by your automation.
I'm just demonstrating what's happening over time.
And then that instance is terminated.
So out of this first part of the automation,
what we have is a patched AMI.
Okay, so how now do we apply this patched AMI
on the auto-scaling group?
Well, we have the opportunity
to run a script directly in your automation a Python script.
So this script is going to update the launch templates
to have a new base AMI for your EC2 instances.
And then we update the auto-scaling group
with the new launch templates, again, from the automation.
But still, this doesn't change all the EC2 instances,
it just make sure that the new EC2 instances
of your auto-scaling group will be launched
with a proper patched AMI.
And so therefore, we must replace all the EC2 instances
of your ASG.
And for this, we're going to use the feature
of auto-scaling group called EC2 instance refresh
that it can, that again can be launched
and started from your automation.
So as you can see here, an SSM automation allows us
to do a very complex flow, interact with many different APIs
of AWS, and everything is managed directly from SSM.
Alright, that's it. I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 34. [SAA/DVA] SSM Parameter Store Overview
# Section: Managing EC2 at Scale - Systems Manager (SSM)
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512812
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the SSM Parameter Store.
It's a secure storage for your configuration
and your secrets.
And optionally,
you can choose to encrypt these configurations
and therefore make it secrets
by using the KMS service.
SSM Parameter Store is serverless,
it's scalable, it's durable,
and the SDK is very easy to use.
On top of it, if you update your parameters
then you have version tracking of them.
The security is provided through IAM
and you get notifications with Amazon EventBridge,
in certain amount of cases.
You have full integration with CloudFormation.
That means that CloudFormation can leverage the parameters
from parameter store as input parameters for your stacks.
So let's take an example.
We have an application
and then we have the SSM parameter store.
So we can store plain text configuration in this way.
Then the IAM permissions of your applications
are going to be checked.
For example, your EC2 instance role
or you can have encrypted configuration.
In that case
the SSM parameter store is going to encrypt it with KMS.
And so the KMS service is going to be used
for encryption and decryption.
And of course, you need to make sure
that your applications do have access
to the underlying KMS key to perform that encryption
and that decryption.
So you can store parameters in the parameter store
with a hierarchy.
So for example, you can define my department
as a path and underneath the My-app and then the Dev
and then we have the Dev DB-URL
and then the DB-password within that folder.
So that means that your parameters goes all the way down
into the hierarchy.
We can go one level up and store a parameter
for the Prod DB-URL, as well as a Prod DB password
and go up to another app or another department.
That really allows you to organize your parameters
the way you want in a structured fashion.
And then this is going to simplify your IAM policies to
allow applications to have access to an entire department,
or to an entire app,
or just to an app department environment specific path.
You also have the opportunity
to access Secrets of Secrets Manager
through the Parameter Store
by using this reference right here.
So it's a little trick that not many people know.
And there are something called Public Parameters
that are issued by AWS that you can use.
For example, if you want to find the latest AMI
for the Amazon Index 2 in your specific region.
This is something that's available
within the Parameter Store as an API call.
So if you take an application,
for example our Dev Lambda function is going to have
an IAM roll that allows it to access
the DB-URL and DB-password within the Dev of my app.
And then if you have a Prod Lambda Function,
thanks to again, a different IAM policy
and maybe some environment variables,
you can access the Prod DB-URL
and Prod DB-password of another path.
(mouse clicks)
Now, within Systems Manager,
you have two kinds of parameter tiers.
You have the standard and the advanced tier.
So the big difference is going to be around the size
of 4KB which is 8KB,
and also the availability of a parameter policy.
For the standard one, we have none but for advanced,
we have some.
The advanced type of parameters
is going to be a $0.05 per month.
Whereas the first one is going to be free.
So what are these parameter policies?
And this is only for advanced parameters.
(mouse clicks)
Well, this allows you to assign a time to live
to a parameter, that means an expiration date.
So that you forced users to update
or delete sensitive data such as passwords.
And you can assign multiple policies at a time.
So here is an example policy.
So this is an expiration policy to delete a parameter
and you say, "Hey, on this time stamp
you must delete these parameter."
And then through the EventBridge integration,
EventBridge is going to get notifications of it.
So in this example, 15 days before the parameter expires
we'll receive notification in EventBridge
which gives us enough time to actually update it
and make sure the parameter is not getting deleted
because of the TTL.
Or maybe sometimes you wanna make sure the parameters
change once in a while.
So you can have a no change notification in EventBridge
so that if a parameter has not been updated for 20 days,
then you will be notified as well.
So you can get very, you know,
creative with the parameter store.
But now you get the idea behind it.
So I hope you like this lecture
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 36. SSM Fleet Manager
# Section: Managing EC2 at Scale - Systems Manager (SSM)
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53218447
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about SSM Fleet Manager.
So it is just a way for you to centrally
and remotely manage all your nodes on AWS or on-premises.
So that includes your EC2 instances,
your on-premises servers
or virtual machines, your Edge devices, and IoT devices.
It supports different operating systems
such as Windows and Linux,
and all nodes must have the SSM agent installed
for them to communicate with the SSM service.
So the idea is that if you have an EC2 instance,
that's mostly gonna be the use case.
You must have an EC2 instance role
with a proper permission called
the Amazon SSM Managed Instance Core permissions
so that they can communicate with a fleet manager service.
Or you can use a feature that prevents you from using this
that makes it even easier called the
Default Host Management Configuration feature.
And so the use case for Fleet Manager on top of
seeing all your instances and manage them all at once
is that you can track the node status,
health and performance.
You can perform troubleshooting and management tasks
and you can perform Windows RDP
or use Session Manager for CLI access
to your Linux based instances.
And Fleet Manager is going to be at the core
of using all the other features of SSM to apply actions
to your instances at scale.
So for the IAM permissions of SSM,
the Amazon SSM Manage Instance Core policy will provide the
necessary permission to your EC2 instances
for registering them with a systems manager in fleet manager
for accessing session manager SSM documents
and SSM parameters, for receiving commands
such as the Run command
and for allowing patch operations
such as using the patch manager feature of SSM,
as well as reports its data to inventory compliance
and the configuration status to SSM.
So as you can see, attaching these permissions
to your EC2 instances is very important.
All right, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 37. SSM Default Host Management Configuration (DHMC)
# Section: Managing EC2 at Scale - Systems Manager (SSM)
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53219079
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk
about the Default Host Management Configuration feature
for Systems Manager or DHMC.
The idea is that we know
that to enable access to Systems Manager,
our EC2 instances must have an IAM role with SSM access.
But it turns out that you can also do without.
So if you configure DHMC, then your EC2 instances
can be automatically managed instances without the use
of an EC2 instance profile.
So how does this work?
Well, we have an instance identity role,
which is a type of IAM role that has no permissions.
And this is for every EC2 instance that you create
but you don't control it.
And the role of this identity role
is to just identify the EC2 instance
to some AWS services, such as Systems Manager.
So this instance identity role is different
from your EC2 instance profile, okay?
It's just something that is on every EC2 instance
but you don't have control over it.
But what's going to happen is that thanks
to this instance identity role,
the EC2 instance identifies with Systems Manager,
which in return is going to pass an IAM role
to the EC2 instance, which will allow the EC2 instance
to be managed by Systems Manager.
And again, all of this is done outside
of the EC2 instance profile.
So for this to work,
you need to have the metadata version two enabled
and the SSM agent enabled that is updated enough
so it doesn't support IMDSv1.
Once the instance is managed by Systems Manager,
it will automatically enable all the features
of Systems Manager,
such as Session Manager, Patch Manager, and Inventory.
And on top of it,
the SSM agent will be automatically kept up to date.
This must be enabled on a per region basis.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk about SSM session manager,
which is a way for you to start a secure shell environment
on your EC2 instances and on-premises servers,
but you access it through the console,
the CLI or the session manager SDK,
and the real power of session manager is that you do not
need to get direct SSH access into your instances. Okay.
Neither using a bastion host or SSH key.
So this is different from the SSH traditional SSH,
or even the EC2 instance connect
that is in the backend using SSH. Okay.
So how does that work?
Where are EC2 instance is running the SSM agents
and is having the right permissions to be registered
with this SSM service.
And so our user is going to connect to the session manager
service with a correct IAM permission, of course.
And then the session manager will be able to execute
commands on our EC2 instance.
So it's using the same mechanism if you want,
as the run commands, the service feature. Okay.
But this time,
the session manager is used to just have a common shell
against our EC2 instance.
The cool thing is that it supports Linux, macOS and windows.
Okay. And all the connections, your instances,
and the executed commands are going to be logged.
So you can have them being sent to Amazon S3 or
CloudWatch Logs.
And the idea is that you have more control
and more security.
When someone does an SSH command into an EC2 instance,
you do not have the history of all the commands

the StartSession events,
which is when session and measure is being used to start a

And optionally,
you can restrict even restrict commands that the user

if you wanted to go deep down the security route.

well we have to open up our security group and our user with

Now let's learn about load balancing.
And a question you may have is what is load balancing?
Well, a load balancer is going to be a server
or a set of servers that will forward traffic
that is received to multiple backend
or downstream EC2 instances or servers.
So the idea is that for example,
we have three EC2 instances
and they're going to be
fronted by an elastic load balancer,
which is a set of servers behind the scenes.
Now, what happens when you have, for example,
three users directly connecting into
your elastic load balancer?
Well, the first one is going to have its
load being sent in one backend EC2 instance
and because there's load balancing well,
if another user is connecting to your elastic load balancer,
then it will be sent to another EC2 instance.
And then finally,
while if a third user is connecting to
your elastic load balancer,
that user will again be load balance
and sense to the third EC2 instance.
So the idea is that the more users you have,
the more the load is going to be balanced across
EC2 instances.
But the idea is that your users do not know
which backend instances they're connected to.
They just know that they have to connect to your
elastic load balancer,
which gives them one end point of connectivity only.
Now,
why should you use a load balancer
where you spread the load across
multiple downstream instances,
you're going to expose a single point of access
to your applications as I just said.
You're going to seamlessly handle failures
of downstream instances
because the load balancer will have
some health check mechanisms
and can understand to which instances

You can do health checks on your instances.
You can provide SSL termination.

high availability across zones
and separate public traffic,
from private traffic on your cloud.
And we'll explore these concepts obviously in a deeper dive.
So the elastic load balancer is a managed load balancer

AWS will be managing it,
and we'll guarantees that it will be working no matter what.

and high availability.

The idea is that using an elastic load balancer is a

because if it's not working properly,

# 55. [SAA/DVA] Elastic Load Balancer - Sticky Sessions
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Let's talk about sticky sessions
or so-called session affinity
for your elastic load balancer.
So it's possible to implement
what's called stickiness or sticky sessions.
And the idea is that the client
doing two requests to the load balancer
will have the same instance in the backend
to respond to the request.
So the idea is that, for example, you have the ALB
with two EC2 instances and you have three clients.
If the client one makes a request
and it goes to the first EC2 instance,
that means that when it does a second request
to the load balancer, it will go to the same instance,
which is a different behavior
where usually the application balancer
will do a spread of all the requests
across all the EC2 instances.
Now for client two, if it goes to the ALB
and talks to the second instance,
then all the requests will go there.
And same for client three, okay?
So this can be enabled for the Classic Load Balancer
Application Balancer and Network Load Balancer.
And how it works, well, there is a cookie
that is sent as part of the request
from the clients to the load balancer
and it has stickiness and it has an expiration date.
That means that when the cookie expires,
then the client may be redirected to another EC2 instance.
The use case for this is to make sure
that the user is connected to the same backend instance
in order not to lose his session data,
which can take some important information
such as the login of the user, for example.
But if you enable stickiness,
it may bring imbalance to the load
over the backend EC2 instances
in case some instances I have a very, very sticky user.
Okay, now to go a little bit deeper,
how about the cookie itself?
Well, there are two types of cookie
that you can have for sticky sessions.
The first one is application-based cookie
and the second one is duration-based cookie.
So for application-based cookies,
well, it's a custom cookie that is generated by the target,
so by your application itself.
And you can include any custom attributes you want
required by your application.
The cookie name must be specified individually
for each target group, okay?
And you may not, you must not use the following names,
so AWSALB, AWSALBAPPOR or AWSALBTG,

And this time will be generated by the load balancer itself,

and it's a cookie generated by the load answer,
and the name is AWSALB for the ALB
and AWSELB for the CLB, okay?
And the idea is this one,
will have an expiry based on a specific duration,
and the duration is generated
by the load balancer itself, okay?
Whereas before, while there is an application-based cookie,
so the duration can be specified by the application itself.
So that's how it works, okay?
You don't need to remember exactly the name of the cookies

# 59. [SAA/DVA] Elastic Load Balancer - Connection Draining
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/26120964
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about a feature
that can come up in the exam,
which is called Connection Draining.
So it has two names, actually.
If you're using a Classic Load Balancer,
it is called Connection Draining,
but if you're using an Application Balancer
or a Network Load Balancer,
this is called a Deregistration Delay.
And the idea behind this concept is that
it will give some time for your instances
to complete the inflight request or the active request
while the instance is being deregistered
or marked unhealthy.
And once a connection is being drained,
so once an instance is being drained,
then the ELB will stop sending your request
to the EC2 instance that is being drained
while being deregistered.
So let's have a look at a diagram to understand better.
So we have three EC2 instances
and in one of them we'll set it in draining mode.
So the users that are already connected to that EC2 instance
are going to be given enough time,
which is the draining period, okay,
to complete their existing connection
and to complete their existing request.
And then once everything's done,
then all the connections will be shut down.
Now, if new users try to connect to our ELB,
our ELB is smart enough to know
that because our EC2 instance is in draining state,
then it will only establish new connections
with other EC2 instances, for example,
my second EC2 instance or my third EC2 instance.
Now you can parametrize
these Connection Draining parameters.
So you can set it anywhere between 1 to 3,600 seconds.
By default, it is 300 seconds, so five minutes,
and you can disable it altogether
if you set the value to zero,
which means that there's no draining happening.
Now, if you set it to low value, okay, this is good
if your requests are short, for example, if there were very,
very short requests for, let's say, less than one second,
well, it's a good idea to set
the draining connection parameter to maybe 30 seconds, okay,
because then this will allow your EC2 instance
to be drained really fast and then be taken offline,
maybe to be replaced or something like this.
If your request can be quite long, for example,
if you have uploads or long lived requests,
then you want to set it to something pretty high,
but the trade-off is that's your EC2 instance
is not going to go away as soon as soon as possible, okay,
it's going to have to wait
until this Connection Draining period is done, okay?
So this is what you need to know about this setting
at a high level.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 62. Target Group Attributes
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512938
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's have a look at all the options
you can set on a target group because they're necessary
to be known at the exam.
So the first one is the deregistration delay,
and this is a timeout you have specified in seconds,
which is corresponding to the time the load balancer
has to wait before deregistering a target.
And we've seen this before.
Then there is slow start, which is expressed in seconds.
And I'll discuss in the next slide.
There is the routing algorithm.
So there's going to be three algorithms
we'll have a look at in the next slide.
So there's going to be Round Robin,
Least Outstanding Request and then Flow Hash.
Then there is the stickiness settings.
So whether or not it's enabled, the type,
which is application-based or duration-based,
and then the cookie name, the duration in seconds
in terms of that cookie name
or for the ALB cookie, just the duration in seconds
in terms of the expiration period.
So now let's have a look at how slow start
and the different routing algorithm works.
So slow start is a way for you to send traffic gradually
to an EC2 instance, because by default,
whenever your target becomes online on your target group,
it will receive its full share of requests.
So it will start getting many, many requests at a time.
And if you unable slow start mode,
it gives a healthy target a bit of time to warm up
before the load balancer sends a full share of requests.
So the idea is that the load balancer will start at zero
and it will linearly increase the number of requests
that it sends to the target until the slow start mode
is ended, and then it will have its full share.
So here's an example.
If you don't have slow start mode, all of a sudden,
as soon as your EC2 instance is part of your target group
is going to receive a full share of requests,
which may overload the instance directly.
But with slow start mode,
there's going to be a gradual increase.
So at first it will receive one request,
then it will receive two requests,
then it will receive three requests
and so on up until the slow start is over
and then the EC2 instance will be at full capacity.
So there's a target where exit slow starts when the duration
period elapses or the target becomes unhealthy.
And if you want to disable slow start,
which is the default setting,
then you just set the slow start duration value to zero.
Now let's have a look at routing algorithms
for your request.
So there's one called the least outstanding request,
which is the next instance to receive the request
is the instance that has the lowest number of pending
or unfinished requests.
So basically, the instance that is the least currently busy
is the instance that will receive the next request,
which makes sense, right?
Because you want to make sure that if an instance
has less requests than another,
then maybe it has more capacity to receive these requests.
So it's available for the ALB and the CLB.
And so the idea is that the first request
will go maybe to the first instance,
the second request to the second
and then the third request has to go to the third
because the third instance right now
doesn't have any requests,
so it has the least outstanding request.
So this is how it works.
And then the fourth one may go again to the third instance
if the third instance has the least outstanding request,
maybe the third request was very, very quick to finish
and so the fourth one went again
to the third instance and so on, okay?
Now for the Round Robin, this is a bit different.
So the Round Robin is that the targets
will have one after the other then next request,
regardless of how many outstanding requests
are available on your instance.
And so this works for ALB and CLB.
The idea is that number one will go to number one,
number two will go to number two
and number three will go to number one,
and then number four will again go through the same cycle.
So number one and so on.
Then for the NLB, there's the flow hash request routing,
which a target is selected based on the hashing
of the protocol, source destination IP address,
source destination ports, and TCP sequence number.
That means that each TCP or UDP connection
is going to be routed for a single target
for the life of the connection,
which is sort of the equivalent for the sticky sessions
on the network load balancer.
So very, very simply, whenever a user makes a request
on EC2 instance, all the information I just said below
is going to be hashed through a flow hash algorithm.
And then thanks to this hash number, is going to route
the same request from the same user to the same EC2 instance
as long as the TCP connection is open, okay?
And this is specificity of your NLB.
So if you go into your target group action
and then edit attributes,
then we're going to see the deregistration delay, okay?
We know this one, the slow start duration.
So by default it's disabled but you can set it, for example,
30 to start enabling it, okay?
Up to 900 seconds, if you really want a slow start duration.
But if you have this, as you can see,
this attribute can now be combined with the least
outstanding request algorithm.
So we'll disable it.
And if you do disabled it,
then we have the least outstanding request algorithm, okay?
That's available, so Round Robin is the default,
but we can have this one, which is again
to send the request to the EC2 instance
that has the least amount of requests available.
So the one that is the least busy right now.
So that's pretty cool.
And then finally, stickiness can be enabled or disabled.
We've seen this before as well.
So that's it, you've seen all the attributes
for your target group.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 63. ALB Rules - Deep Dive
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512942
# Caption: en_US (manual)

(Instructor) So a quick lecture
to understand rules as a whole.
So rules are set up on your application load balancer
and you can have many rules or one rule too,
and the last rule is called the default rule
and each rule will have a specific target. Okay?
Now, the rules are going to be processed in order. Okay?
The default rule is going to be the last one to be processed
and each rule supports different actions.
For example, it can forward to a specific target group,
it can redirect to a specific other URL,
or it can send a fixed response back.
Rules can have conditions in terms of which rule is
going to be hit first.
So, it could be having a rule on the host header. Okay?
This is part of the client request.
It could be an HTTP request method to see if the request is
a GET or a POST, or a PUT.
The path pattern, so where the request is sent to,
is it slash my app 1 or slash my app 2.
Source IP, so what, where's the request coming from.
And a specific HTTP header in general,
or the query string parameters as part of the request.
So this really allows you to create some complex routing to
different target groups based on certain conditions
on the originating request.
Another thing you should know is that for a single rule,
as part of your ALB, you could have
multiple target groups as a target.
And the idea is that you can specify weights for each
target group within a single rule.
So the idea behind this is that you want to be able to
evolve your backend services, okay,
from one target group to another, and to update them.
And so you want to have version one in one target group
and version two in another target group.
And you want to evaluate whether or not
version two make sense.
This is also called a blue green deployment.
So thanks to this weighting,
you can control how much traffic goes from your ALB to
a specific target group as part of a rule.
So let's have a look at an example.
So let's say that we have our users,
they talked to the ALB and the ALB has been wired to talk to
target group one historically. Okay.
Which is your blue group,
but now you're going to add a target group two,
which is a new version of your application.
And you will set up weights in your rule.
You have a weight of eight, for target group one
and a weight of two for target group two.
That means that now for a single rule,
the ALB will send 80% of the traffic to your first group and
20% of the traffic to the second group,
which would allow you to do some monitoring on your target
groups and to see whether or not they are receiving the
traffic correctly,
whether or not the metrics are good, and whether or not your
application version is behaving as expected. Okay?
So this is a cool new feature as well.

# 64. [SAA/DVA] Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) Overview
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27512980
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
what is an auto scaling group.
So when we deploy a website or an application,
the load can change over time because we may have
more users visiting our websites over time.
And we've seen that in the cloud, in AWS,
it's possible for us to create
and also get rid of servers very quickly
with the EC2 instance creation API call.
So, if you wanna automate this,
we can create an auto-scaling group.
So the goal of the ASG is to scale out,
that means add EC2 instances and you need to remember this,
scale out to match an increased load
or to scale in that means removing EC2 instances
to match a decreased load.
And so therefore the size of our ASG
is going to vary over time.
Overall, we can also define parameters
to ensure we'll have a minimum
and a maximum number of EC2 instances running at any time
in our ASG.
ASG also have the superpower
that if you are pairing it with a load balancer,
then any EC2 instances as part of the ASG
will be linked to the load balancer.
Another superpower is that
if one instance is deemed unhealthy, it is terminated
and a new EC2 instance is created to replace it.
So, auto scaling groups are free
and you're only going to pay
for whatever resources are created underneath
such as your EC2 instances.
So let's see how an ESG works in AWS.
So we set a minimum capacity,
which is how many instances you want at minimum in your ASG.
For example, two.
Then you set a desired capacity,
which is how many instances you want in your ASG,
for example, four and then you set a maximum capacity
which is how many instances
at a maximum do I want in my ASG.
And then that means that if you move the desire capacity
to higher number,
but that's still less than a maximum capacity,
then you can scale out as needed.
That means scale out means adding EC2 instances
and so therefore your ASG can grow bigger
and bigger and bigger.
In this instance, the maximum capacity is seven.
As I said, the ASG also works with a load balancer.
So if we have four instances registered in our ASG,
then the ELB is going to distribute traffic
to all these instances right away
and so your users can access a load balanced website.
But the ELB also has the ability
to check for the health of your EC2 instances
using the health check
and that health check can be passed on to the ASG.
That means that the ASG can terminate EC2 instances
if they are deemed unhealthy by the load balancer,
which is very handy.
Also, if you scale out, that means if you add EC2 instances,
then of course the ELB is going to send traffic
to them as well and spread the load.
Therefore, it's a really great combination
to use a load balancer and an auto scaling group.
Now, in terms of attributes to create your ASG,
you need to create a launch template.
There used to be a thing called launch configurations
but it's deprecated, but the idea is the same.
A launch template contains information
on how to launch EC2 instances within your ASG.
So you have information about the AMI
and the instance type, the EC2 user data,
the EBS volumes, security groups, SSH key pair,
IAM roles for your EC2 instances,
network and subnet information
as well as load balancer information and more if you want.
And so all these parameters look a lot like
the ones we specified when we created an EC2 instance.
On top of it, your ASG has a min size,
a max size and an initial capacity we need to define
as well as scaling policies.
Talking about scaling policies,
let's see how CloudWatch alarm integrates with auto scaling.
So you don't know what CloudWatch is yet of course,
but let me just tell you a little bit about it right now.
So it's possible to scale in and out,
an ASG based on CloudWatch alarms.
So for example, we have an ASG right here
with three EC2 instances
and the alarm is going to be triggered
and therefore we're going to get a scale out activity.
So what would trigger an alarm?
Well, it's a metric you can return, for example,
for the average CPU or any custom metric you want.
So for example, if the average CPU
as a whole for your ASG is too high,
then you need to add EC2 instances
and therefore the alarm is going to be triggered
and is going to trigger a scaling activity
in your auto scaling group
and this is why it's called an auto scaling group
because paired with alarms,
there is an automatic aspect of scaling behind the scenes.
So based on the alarm, we can create scale out policies.
That means increasing the number of instances
or we can create scale in policies
to decrease the number of instances.
And all these things together are what composes ASG.

# 66. [SAA/DVA] Auto Scaling Groups - Scaling Policies
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27513020
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we have several scaling policies
for auto scaling group.
The first one is dynamic scaling and within this category,
we have the target tracking scaling,
which is very simple to set up.
The idea is that you define a metric for your ASG,
for example, the CPU utilization
and you define a target value, for example, 40%.
And automatically, the ASG is going to scale out or in
to allow you to keep this metric to around 40%.
We also have the simple or step scaling
and the idea is that you define CloudWatch alarms
that are being triggered when you want to add units
of capacity to your auto scaling group
or when you want to remove units of capacity
to your auto scaling group.
Then we have scheduled scaling.
So this is when you anticipate a scaling
based on a known usage pattern.
For example, you say that you know that every time
at 5:00 PM on Fridays, you're going to get new users
and therefore, you want to increase
the minimum capacity to 10.
Then we have predictive scaling.
So this is when you continuously forecast load
and then you start scheduling ahead of time.
So this is very good when you have patterns
that repeat themselves.
So automatically, the ASG is going to analyze
historical load then generate a forecast
and then schedule scaling actions based on the forecast,
which can be very handy if you have cyclical data.
So some good metrics to scale on is a big question.
So it depends really on what your application is doing
and how it's working.
But usually, here are a few.
So number one is CPU utilization,
because every time your instance receive a request,
usually, they will do some sort of computation
and so it will use some CPU.
And so if you look at the average CPU utilization
across all your instances and it goes higher,
that means that your instances are being more utilized.
And so it would be a good metric to scale on.
Another metric to scale on, it's more application-specific,
but it is a RequestCountPerTarget,
which is based on your testing,
you know that your EC2 instances operate
at an optimal request of 1,000 requests
per target at a time and so maybe this is the target
you want to have for your scaling.
So here as an example.
You have an auto scaling group with three EC2 instances
and your ALB is currently spreading the request
across all of them.
So right now the value of the request counts
per target metric is three,
because each EC2 instance, on average,
has three requests outstanding.
Next if your application is network-bound,
so for example there's a lot of uploads and downloads
and you know that network is going to be a bottleneck
for your EC2 instances,
then you may want to scale on the average network in or out
to make sure that if you reach some certain threshold,
then you're going to scale based on that.
Or any custom metric that you push to CloudWatch,
so you can set up your own metrics
that are going to be application-specific
and based on that, you can set up your scaling policies.
Now one last thing you need to know about scaling policies
is what's called a scaling cooldown.
So the idea is that after there is a scaling activity,
so whenever you add or you remove instances,
you are entering the cooldown period,
which is, by default, five minutes or 300 seconds.
And during that cooldown period,
the ASG will not launch or terminate additional instances.
And the reason behind this reasoning
is that you allow for metrics to stabilize,
for your new instance to enter into effect
and to see what the new metric will become.
So the idea is that when there is a scaling action
that occurs, the question is,
is there a default cooldown in effect?
If yes, then ignore the action.
If no, then proceed with the scaling action,
which is to launch or terminate instances.
And so an advice to you is to use a ready-to-use AMI
to reduce the configuration time for your EC2 instances
in order for them to be serving the request faster.
So if you don't spend time configuring your EC2 instance,
then they can be in effect right away.
And then because they can be active way faster,
then the cooldown period can be decreased
and you can have a more dynamic scaling up and down
of your ASG.
And of course, you need to make sure to enable
something like detailed monitoring for your ASG
to get access to metrics every one minute
and to make sure that you have
these metrics being updated fast enough.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 68. Auto Scaling Groups - Instance Refresh
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53219051
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about a very handy feature
of Auto Scaling groups called Instance Refresh.
So the idea is that you want to update
an entire Auto Scaling group
thanks to a new launch template that you've created.
And so you wanna re-create all EC2 instances.
For this, you can, instead of terminating an instance
and waiting for it to come back,
you can use the native feature of Auto Scaling groups
called Instance Refresh.
So let's take an example.
Say we have an Auto Scaling group
and the EC2 instances have been launched
with an old launch template.
I say old because we are creating a new launch template.
For example, we updated the underlying AMI
of our EC2 instances,
and then we're going to the API call
named Start Instance Refresh.
So what's going to happen is
that we're going to set a minimum healthy percentage,
for example, 60%,
and that tells our Auto Scaling group
how many instances can be deleted over time.
And then as instances are terminated,
then new ones are coming up with the new launch template.
That's why it's called an EC2 Instance Refresh,
is because instances are being terminated
and new ones come up.
And over time, all instances having the old launch template
will be terminated and the new ones will come up.
So on top of it, to make sure that your EC2 instances
have enough time to be ready and to serve traffic,
you can specify a warm-up time,
which is to say how long to wait until we can assume
that the new EC2 instance is ready to use.
Okay? So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 69. Auto Scaling Groups - Warm Pools
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53218419
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about Warm Pools.
And here is the problem.
When you have an auto-scaling group and it scales out,
that means that when you add instances
into your auto-scaling group,
you want to launch instances as fast as possible.
But sometimes your instances,
they're doing some initialization,
they're doing some bootstrapping,
and that can take several minutes before your instances
are actually available to serve traffic.
So it could be also getting some data,
filling in some internal states for such as a cache,
you run configuration scripts, et cetera, et cetera.
So historically,
the solution was to over-provision compute resources
in order to absorb the unexpected demand.
But then this is going to lead to an increased cost
because you're over-provisioned.
Or you try to fit as much as possible into a Golden Image
to try to reduce your boot time.
But none of these are perfect.
And actually you want
to use the auto-scaling group Warm Pools.
So what are these Warm Pools?
Well, the idea is that we have a pool
of pre-initialized instances, and by having this,
we are going to reduce the scale out latency.
So let me explain.
Say we have a auto-scaling group
with a desired capacity of three and a max capacity of six,
then the Warm Pool is going to be of size three.
Three is by default the difference between the max capacity
and the desired capacity.
So six minus three equals three.
That's basically the maximum number of instances
that can be put from the pool into the auto-scaling group
until we reach the max capacity.
And so these instances in the Warm Pool,
they have been pre-initialized.
So all the setup you need has been done.
And then they go into a state.
We'll see the state is either started,
stopped, or hibernated.
But the idea is that whenever you have a scale-out event,
then the new instance is going from the pool
into your auto-scaling group.
So the idea is that by doing this,
the instant that comes into the auto-scaling group
has done some pre-initialization work.
Now let's go into the Warm Pool size setting.
So we have the minimum Warm Pool size.
This is the number of instances you always want
in the Warm Pool no matter what.
Then the max prepared capacity,
either it is equal to the max capacity
of the auto-scaling group.
That means that to see how many instances
you have in your Warm Pool, you do the difference
of the actual desired capacity of the RSG
and the max capacity.
Or if you have, say, for example,
a max capacity of 1500 instances
and a desired capacity of 1000,
you may not want to have 1500 instances
in your Warm Pool.
So you may want to specify just a set number of instances,
for example, 100, so that it remains manageable.
But at small sizes, the default is fine.
Now, the Warm Pool instance states,
so your instances are going to be in a different stage
such as running, stopped, or hibernated.
And you can cache a state
to perform some last minute customization
on your E2 instance as as they're building
rolled from the Warm Pool
into your auto-scaling group itself.
And finally, while the E2 instances are in the Warm Pool,
they don't contribute to your auto-scaling group metrics
that would affect any scaling policies.
So that's it.
We've learned about this feature of the ASG
to scale out faster
and have less initialization time for instances.
So I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 70. ASG for CloudOps
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27513036
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so let's have a look
at a few features you need to know,
going into the SysOps exam.
So, the lifecycle hooks is a way for you
to hook into the lifecycle of an ASG instances.
So that means, whenever it's being initiated and terminated.
So by default, as soon as you create an instance,
it goes into service right away.
So it goes from pending to in service.
But you can set up an lifecycle hook for that effect.
And so it can go into some extra steps.
So after pending, it can go into a pending wait state
as part of your lifecycle hook, okay?
And in that state, you can define a script
to run on the instance as they start.
For example, for some initial setup.
So when you're done with the initial setup
of your EC2 instances,
you make them go into a pending proceed state.
And then after that, they will be moved
into the in service states.
So this lifecycle hook really allows you
to perform some kind of custom logic
between the pending and the in service states.
Then, you can also perform some action
before the instance is terminated.
So for example,
you want to pause the instance
before they're terminated for troubleshooting,
and what this will give you is the opportunity,
for example, to take the logs out of your instances.
So let's say that instance goes from in service
to terminating, then in part of your lifecycle hook, okay,
you can go into the terminating wait state, okay.
And then when you're there,
you can execute again, some scripts,
or get some logs out, or do whatever you want,
or even get some information out, take an AMI,
whatever you want, really.
Or take an EBS snapshot,
and then go into terminating proceed.
And then after this, it will go into the terminated states.
And then, the use-cases for all these lifecycle hooks
is really to do cleanup, log extraction,
or special health checks, before your instance is started
and goes in service.
And to integrate the scripts into these lifecycle hooks,
there's EventBridge, SNS, and SQS.
So whenever there's a lifecycle event trigger,
one, a message can be sent to these three destinations.
And if it goes into even EventBridge, for example,
it can invoke the Lambda function
for you to perform any kind of scripting you want,
on top of things.
Okay, so very quickly, there's launch configuration,
and launch templates.
So, both allow you to specify the AMI,
the instance type, a key pair, security groups,
and any other parameters to launch your EC2 instance,
which has tags and user-data, okay.
And they're both used by your ASG to launch instances.
But you cannot edit them.
So whenever you wanted to create a new launch configuration,
you actually create a new one, and launch template,
you have to create a new version.
So launch configuration must be recreated every single time.
They're part of their legacy of AWS,
so they are not used anymore, really.
And launch templates are newer,
so they can have multiple versions,
which is a much cleaner way
of evolving your launch templates.
They can create parameter subsets,
so you can have launch templates
based on other launch templates
for configuration reuse and inheritance.
You can provision both on-demand and spot instances
as part of your launch templates,
or a mix, to have a fleet that's going to be optimized.
You cannot do this with launch configuration.
It supports placement groups, capacity reservation,
dedicated hosts, and multiple instance types.
And you can use the T2 unlimited burst feature.
So this is the recommended thing to use,
going forward by AWS.
Next, you can look at your SQS with auto-scaling.
So how to scale, and it's gonna group,
based on an SQS queue status.
So, in this example we have an SQS queue,
and a bunch of EC2 instances processing messages from it.
And what you want to do, is to scale your ASG
based on whether or not you have more messages
in your SQS queue.
So for this, you can create a CloudWatch metric.
For example, on the queue length.
So the metric name is approximate number of messages.
And whenever that queue length is too big,
that means you have too many messages to process.
Then you can create an alarm,
and that alarm will go into CloudWatch alarm,
and would be triggering a scaling policy
on your ASG.
Now for your ASG, your multiple health checks.
So, to make sure you have the high availability,
and you need to have at least two instances
in your ASG, okay, in multi-AZ ASG.
And then you can do some health checks,
such as the EC2 status checks.
So, to make sure that the underlying software
and hardware of your EC2 instances are still functioning,
which is enabled by default.
But also the ELB health check.
So this is to make sure that your application,
if linked to a target group and an ALB will be checked,
will be having its health checked by the ELB as well.
And in case, while the ELB figures out
that your instance is unhealthy,
then your ASG will terminate it.
And there's one last type of health check,
which is called the custom health check,
which is to send the instance health
to the ESG manually, or automatically,
using the CLI or the SDK.
So there is an API call for you
to set the instance health directly on your ASG.
That's why it's called the custom health check.
So, whenever a health check is not passing,
then the instance will be deemed unhealthy.
And a new instance will be launched
after terminating an unhealthy one.
There will not be a reboot of unhealthy hosts for you.
So, if the instance is failing its EC2 status check,
then it will not reboot the instance.
It will just terminate it and launch a new one.
So, good to know CLI is set instance health.
So this is the API call that's being used
for the custom health checks.
And terminate-instance-in-auto-scaling-group,
as well as another one that you should be using.
Finally, some common troubleshooting around your ASG.
So if you have already, some instances running in your ASG,
but you cannot launch any new EC2 instances,
it could be for example,
that while your auto-scaling group has reached a limit
that you set by your maximum capacity parameter,
in which case you have more instances,
you need to increase the maximum capacity
for you as you to scale out more.
Another also common problem
for new instances not being launched,
is that you have a capacity issue in the AZ.
And so therefore, because the ASG cannot find capacity,
then the instance cannot be launched.
Then, if launching a specific EC2 instance is failing,
maybe the security group does not exist.
So it might've been deleted in the backend.
So, have a look for this.
Or the key pair does not exist.
It might've been deleted as well.
And if there is issues for your ASG to launch instances
over 24 hours, then it will suspend the processes
of auto-scaling, which is a suspension that's automatic
for you to debug, okay?
So that's it for an overview of the things you need to know,
going into the exam as a SysOps.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 72. Auto Scaling Overview
# Section: EC2 High Availability and Scalability
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27513044
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So are the backbone of Auto Scaling
is the AWS Auto Scaling Service.
So it's going to be available for all the
scalable resources in AWS.
So Auto Scaling groups obviously to allow you
to launch or terminate EC2 instances.
But also Spot Fleet requests,
to launch or terminate instances
from a Spot Fleet request itself.
And to automatically replace instances that get interrupted
for price or capacity reasons.
You have Amazon ECS that will be leveraging Auto Scaling
to adjust the ECS service desired count up and down.
DynamoDB tables for your tables or your global
secondary indexes to adjust the WCU and RCU.
So write capacity units and read capacity units over time.
And Aurora will be using Auto Scanning as well
for Dynamic Read Replica Auto Scaling, okay?
And obviously, maybe other services as well
will be added over time to the Auto Scaling service in AWS.
So we have Scaling Plans and it can be dynamic scaling.
We start knowing it already to track a target itself.
So without dynamic scaling,
you have the same capacity over time.
But with dynamic scaling,
you start adjusting the capacity over time.
And so you stabilize the utilization of your service itself.
So you can optimize for availability in which case
40% of your research utilization will be the target.
You can balance, and so this will be about 50% utilization.
Or if you want to optimize for cost,
then you will have 70% of resource utilization.
But obviously the closer you get to 100%,
the less efficient your scaling is going to be
because you're going to reach a performance bottleneck.
And obviously you can choose your own metric
and your own target value
if you didn't want to follow the recommendations
provided by AWS.
And options for dynamic scaling is to disable scale-in.
So that means you can only scale out, but not scale-in.
You can specify the cool-down period,
as well as the warmup time for the ASG.
And opposite to dynamic scaling is predictive scaling.
So we know this already.
So with predictive scaling, the idea is that
you're going to analyze the historical loads
using a machine learning algorithm done by AWS for you,
and then a forecast will be generated
and then scheduling extras will be taken automatically
based on that forecast.

# 75. [DVA] CloudFormation - Overview
# Section: CloudFormation for CloudOps
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/12905198
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's learn about AWS CloudFormation,
which is one of my personal favorite services in AWS.
So CloudFormation is a way for you to outline
your AWS infrastructure for any resources for this
using just code.
For example, in a CloudFormation template,
you're going to say, I want a security group.
I want two EC2 instances
that are going to be using the security group.
I want Elastic IPs for these EC2 instances.
I want an S3 bucket.
I want a load balancer in front of these EC2 instances.
And then by declaring what you want by just saying,
hey, all these things should exist
and they should be linked together, automatically,
CloudFormation will create them for you in the right order
with the exact configuration that you specify.
So this removes any need of doing manual configuration
and manual work, and all the things is provisioned
through CloudFormation.
So a CloudFormation template is going to be some code,
and the code will involve in a declarative way
what you want your infrastructure to be composed of.
And then we'll be able to visualize this infrastructure
using Infrastructure Composer
to see how the components relate to each other
in CloudFormation.
So why should you use AWS CloudFormation?
Well, first, it is your infrastructure as code.
That means that no resources are being manually created,
which is going to be excellent for control.
And all the code that makes up
these CloudFormation templates can be used
for version control, for example, using Git.
Also, any changes to your infrastructure
is going to be reviewed through code changes.
In terms of cost,
well, all the resources within your CloudFormation stack
is going to be tagged with an identifier
so you can easily see how much a CloudFormation stack
is going to cost you.
And we can also estimate the cost of resources
from your CloudFormation templates.
And finally, you can have saving strategy.
For example, in your development environment,
you could automate the deletion of the templates at 5:00 PM
and recreate them automatically at 8:00 AM in a safe matter
because everything is automated.
For productivity,
this is amazing because you have the ability to destroy
and recreate an infrastructure on the cloud on the fly.
And this is really leveraging the whole power of the cloud,
which is to just create and delete things
and only pay as you go.
You also have automated generation of diagrams
for your template, which is very good
for your architecture diagrams
and its declarative programming.
So you don't need to figure out the order of the creation
of the resources and the orchestration of things.
All these things are done by CloudFormation for you.
There's also a separation of concern.
You can create many CloudFormation stacks
for many applications and many layers.
For example, you may want to have stacks
for your network and your VPCs.
You may want to have stacks for your applications and so on.
Finally, you don't reinvent the wheel
because you can leverage existing templates on the web
and the documentation
to quickly write your CloudFormation templates.
Now, how does CloudFormation work?
Well, your templates must be uploaded in Amazon S3
and then referenced from CloudFormation.
So you upload it, and then from CloudFormation
you reference it and a stack will be created.
And what is a CloudFormation stack?
Well, it is made of AWS resources,
and it could be any kind of things you can create on AWS.
If you wanted to update a template,
you cannot edit the previous one.
What we have to do is to re-upload
a new version of the template to AWS
and then update your stack.
Now, your stacks are identified by a name within the region,
and if you delete a CloudFormation stack,
every single artifact and resource
that was created by CloudFormation will be deleted.
Now, how do we deploy CloudFormation templates?
Well, there is the manual way
in which we're going to use something
like Infrastructure Composer
or a code editor to directly create
our CloudFormation templates, and then we use the console
to input the parameters and so on.
And we'll do this method mostly in this course
for learning purposes, or you can go the automated way.
So you're going to edit your templates in a YAML file,
and then you use the CLI to deploy the templates,
or you use a continuous delivery tool
to this automatically on the cloud.
And it's recommended if you want to fully automate your flow
to deploying CloudFormation templates.
Now, the building blocks of CloudFormation.
So your template is made of different components,
and we'll have a look at them in detail,
so don't be overwhelmed by this,
but we have the AWSTemplateFormatVersion,
which defines the version of how to read the templates.
This is for internal purposes from AWS.
The description, which is the comments about the templates,
the resources, which is the actual only mandatory section
in CloudFormation, which is going to define
all the AWS resources that are declared in the templates,
the parameters,
which are the dynamic inputs for your templates,
the mappings, the static variables for your templates,
and we'll see the differences
between parameters and mappings,
the outputs to get references to what has been created
in your templates,
conditionals, which are a list of conditions
to perform resource creation,
and we'll have a few template helpers
such as references and functions.
But don't worry.
We'll have a look at all of this
and code examples in this section, so don't worry.
So that's it for an introduction to CloudFormation.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.
