# 282. Roure 53 - Email Record Types
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217611
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk
about common DNS records types for email.
So you don't need to be an expert on this,
but you need to see them once
so that you know what you're talking about
if you see them at one question at the exam.
So the first record is MX and it's for Mail Exchange.
It tells where to deliver inbound mail.
So that means that inbound mail will be received,
for example, by this server, as I put in my example.
Then, you have three types of TXT records.
So TXT is text,
and you can put whatever you want in a TXT record.
So they can be used for different purposes.
The first one is the SPF.
It's important, it's the Sender Policy Framework.
It authorizes which servers are allowed to send mail.
So in my example, I include Amazon SES.
So SES is a service to send mail,
and we're telling the web that this server
is allowed to send mail on our behalf.
The DKIM is DomainKeys Identified Mail.
It's a way to cryptographically verify
the message integrity.
So it's just some text that you have to enter.
And DMARC is a way to define a handling policy
for messages failing the SPF and DKIM.
So, different levels of security,
but all these are texts that you need to include.
You don't have to figure it out.
The email provider will tell you what to do.
But, so in the case of Amazon SES,
to integrate it with Route 53,
first of all, you verify your domain in Amazon SES,
and for this,
you're going to get a TXT record for verification.
Showing that you're able to insert this TXT record
in Route 53
will prove that you have the domain ownership.
Then, you're going to set up DKIM, which is recommended,
and is going to give you three CNAME records
to enter for DKIM signature.
You want to do anything besides just copying and pasting.
Then, you update the Route 53 hosted zone,
where you're going to add the SES verification,
the DKIM records, and the SPF records.
And then the MX records if you're receiving, as well,
email through SES,
and then you wait for propagation.
And then when the DNS records are propagated,
the SES status will change to verified.
So important things to remember from an exam perspective
is that SPF records and DKIM records are TXT records,
and they're helpful for sending emails.
And the MX record is for receiving emails.
Of course, this is all complicated to do.
So there is in Route 53, in Amazon SES,
a button to create everything for you in Route 53
and just wait.
But an exam will expect you
to know what MX and TXT records are
and what SPF and DKM is used for.
All right, that's it.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 283. [SAA/DVA] Route 53 - TTL
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193836
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so let's have a look at TTLs.
So a record TTL is a Time To Live.
And let's take this example where a client is accessing
our DNS Route 53 and a web server.
So we do a DNS request for myapp.example.com,
and we get an answer from the DNS,
which is saying, hey, please, this is an A record.
Here is the IP, and there is a TTL,
maybe a TTL of 300 seconds.
So TTL is saying, hey clients, please cache this result
for the duration of the TTL.
So for 300 seconds,
the client is going to cache the results.
That means that if the client is requesting again
or accessing the same host name,
what's going to happen is that
the client will not issue a query to the DNS system,
because it already knows the answer,
because the answer has been cached,
and we're still within the cache period, so the cache TTL.
The idea behind this
is that we don't want to query the DNS too often,
because we don't expect records to change a lot,
and so, therefore, using the response it has,
the client can access our web server
and do HTTP request and responses.
So we have, you know, two extreme cases.
For example, if you set a high TTL of, say, 24 hours,
then this is going to do a lot less traffic on Route 53,
because less clients are doing requests,
because the result are cached for 24 hours,
and, possibly, while the client will have outdated records.
If somehow you want to change the record,
you will need to wait 24 hours
to make sure that all your clients
will have the new records in their cache.
If you said set a low TTL,
for example, 60 seconds, at the opposite,
then it's going to do a lot more traffic on your DNS,
so a lot more dollar you're going to spend,
because you get price per how many request
do reach Route 53.
But the records will be outdated for less time,
so it's quicker for you to do a record change,
and it's easier to change records overall.
So it's up to you, really,
to see what a good TTL or low TTL is.
If you plan on changing a record,
the idea is that sometimes
you will decrease the TTL for, say, 24 hours,
and then when you know that all the clients
have a new TTL that is low,
then you change the record value
which gets updated for everyone,
and then you increase the TTL.
This is a strategy.
So the TTL is mandatory for every record
except the Alias record that we'll see in the next lecture.
So let's have a look how TTL works in the console.
So let's have a look at how Time To Live works.
So let's create a new record,
and this one is going to be called
demo.stephanetheteacher.com,
and the value of it is going to be
one of the EC2 instances we know.
So let's take the one in eu-central-1.
So I'm gonna take this EC2 instance
and paste the value of it.
And then for the TTL, we're going to set two minutes.
So to do so I'm going to click twice on this minute button.
So the TTL is now 120 seconds.
So let me create this record.
And now my record has been created.
So it is an A record pointing to a specific IP
at demo.stephanetheteacher.com.
Now, I want to show you that the record is working,
but Firefox is not very nice with me.
So if I try to open this in Firefox
it's going to give me a problem.
So this is not something I can fix easily,
so I'm going to use Google Chrome on the right-hand side
to show you this.
So if I do demo.stephanetheteacher.com on Google,
then automatically it should direct me to, yes,
my eu-central-1 instance.
So that means that this record, this A record,
is fully functioning.
And I can also make sure of that,
for example, if I'm using CloudShell.
So if I clear this and do an nslookup
on demo.stephanetheteacher.com,
as you can see, the address is correct.
And if I do a dig command on this, then we get an answer.
And there's a cool number that we're showing here,
so the answer section, there's 115.
So the idea here, that's because I did do a DNS query.
Then the record get cached for 120 seconds.
And if I retype again this dig command right here,
as you can see the number got down to 98.
So that means that for 98 seconds,
actually, I will get the same response,
because, no matter what,
this is what's cached on my computer.
So if I'm very quick

so instead of this IP, I want to go to ap-southeast-1,
so we'll use the first IP in my list and save this.
So even though this record was being updated, okay,
if I go into CloudShell and, again, do this dig command,

That's because for 66 more seconds

And if I go to Chrome, I think I was fast enough,
I go to Chrome and refresh this page,

And this is because, again,
my record got cached for two minutes.
So when the cache is expiring, then only then

And then, again, will I get the answer

So the best way to check it is just to wait.

So now let's have a look at the differences

So CNAME allows you to point a hostname

For example, you can say app.mydomain.com
is pointing to blabla.anything.com.
And this only works if you have a non root domain name,
so if you have something.mydomain.com.
It does not work for just mydomain.com,
as we'll see in the hands-on.
On the other hand, you have alias records,
and these are specific to Route 53,
but they allow you to point a hostname
to a specific AWS Resource.
So app.mydomain.com is pointing to blabla.amazonaws.com.
And these resources we'll see in a second where they are.
But these alias records work
for both root domains and non root domains.
So you can have mydomain.com pointing
to, as an alias, to an alias resource
which is very, very good.

So on top of it, alias is very good

and they have a native health check capability within them.

they are only mapped to resources in AWS.

# 285. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - Simple
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193846
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about routing policies
for Route 53.
So a routing policy is helping Route 53
respond to DNS queries,
and we shouldn't be confused about the word routing.
This is not like when you have a load balancer and the
actual load balancer will route traffic
to the backend EC2 instances.
No, no, no.
This routing is from a DNS perspective.
So the DNS does not respond, does not route any traffic.
So the traffic doesn't go through the DNS.
The DNS only will respond to the DNS queries
and then the clients will know to which way
they should be doing these HTTP queries, for example.
So the DNS just helps translate host names
into actual endpoints that the clients can use.
So Route 53 will support the following routing policy.
There's simple, weighted, failover, latency based,
geolocation, multi-value answer, and geoproximity.
And we're going to have a look at all of them
in this section.
So the first one is going to be the simple routing policy.
And the idea is that with this,
that we've actually been using before,
we're going to route traffic to a single resource typically.
So here's an example.
The clients that will say, hey,
I want to go to foo.example.com,
and Routes 53 will say, hey,
go to this IP address.
And this is an A record.
So it is possible for us to specify multiple values
in the same record.
And if so, if multiple values are returned by the DNS,
then a random one will be chosen by the clients
or client side.
So in this example,
we have the client's asking again for foo.example.com,
and Amazon Route 53 will just reply with three IP addresses
that occur embedded into the A record.
And then the clients will pick one of them randomly
and apply it for the routing.
So if you have enabled an alias record alongside
the simple policy,
then you can only specify on AWS resource as a target.
And finally, it's called simple because it's very simple.
And therefore you can not associate this with health checks
and we'll see health checks later on in this section
and how they work.
So let's go in the console to see how a routing policy
of step simple can be created.
So let's create a record, and the record name is going to be
simple.stephanetheteacher.com.
It's an A record, and the value of which is going to be,
for example, my instance in ap-southeast-1.
Now for TTL, it will say something very low,
like 20 seconds.
And the routing policy is going to be here.
So as you can see, we have different possibilities,
six of them, and then one other that is
somewhere else in the UI.
So we have a TTL 20 seconds as simple writing policy,
and let's just create this record.
So we've been doing this before.
We know how this works.
So now if we go to simple.stephanetheteacher.com.
And go to this URL, we get
Hello World from my instance in ap-southeast-1b,
which is awesome.
And if we do a dig command and have a look,
so we need to reinstall dig.
So sudo yum install bind-utils.
So this is because I restarted my machine here.
Okay, we're going to redo the dig command.
So we do the dig command on this.
As we can see, we have an A record of a TTL of 20 seconds
pointing to this IP.
But we can change this record now.
We're going to edit the record.
So I will just simply click on it and edit the record.
And for the value, now, I can enter multiple IPs.
So I can insert my one in ap-southeast-1
or one in us-east-1, for example.
So when I do so and save this,
what's going to happen is that once the TTL expires
from before, we're going to get two records back.
So let's use CloudShell to verify this.
So I'm going to do a dig command.
And as you can see,
now we have in the intersection, we have two responses.
We have one in this IP and one in this IP.
So it's a client side choice.
So that means that if I go to this website and refresh,

And I didn't.
So I was back into ap-southeast-1b,
but let me pause for 20 seconds and I'll get back to you.

# 286. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - Weighted
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193852
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the weighted routing policy.
The idea is that you can have a percentage of requests
you can control to go to a specific resource
thanks to weights.
So, put it simply in the diagram,
we have Amazon route 53,
and then we have three EC2 instance
that have been assigned different weights,
so 70, 20, and 10.
In my example, these weights sum up to 100,
but you don't have to in the real life, okay?
But what this means that 70%
of the DNS responses from Amazon as on route 53
are going to be redirecting to the first EC2 instance,
then 20% to the second and 10% to the third.
So what we have to do in our weight is to assign each record
a relative weights.
And then the traffic percentage is going to be sent
to each record, as just the weight of the record
divided by the sum of all the weights of all the records
which is like a percentage of all the weights, okay?
The weights don't need to sum up to 100,
they're just indicative of how much
we want to send to this instance,
compared to all the other records in your DNS name.
So to make this work,
the DNS records must have the same name and type,
and you can associate them with health checks,
although we haven't seen with health checks are again yet,
but we'll have a look at them very, very soon.
Now the use cases for a weighted routing policy
is pretty obvious, is to do for example, load balancing,
maybe across different regions, or to test a new application
version by sending a small amount of traffic to it,
and so on.
And then if you're sending to sort of a weight of zero,
then you're going to stop sending traffic
to a specific resource, so you can shift weight over time.
And if all the resource records will have a weight of zero,
then all the records will be returned with equal weights.
So let's have a look in the console
to see how that works.

So as we can see,
we can associate a health check with it,

And we have a record ID that we can set.
And this is to identify this specific record
within the weighted record sets.
So for this one, I got this instance from the southeast,
I'm just going to write southeast.
Okay, and then we can add another record.
And again, we're going to use the same
weighted.stephanetheteache.com, okay?
And the routing policy is going to be weighted.
And the value of which is going to be
the one from us-east-1.
So I'm going to copy this IP and paste it here.
The weight is going to be on this time 70.
So we're going to send 70% of the traffic to us-east-1,
and then the record ID is US East.
Great, and the TTL again, three seconds.
And one last record we're going to add, so again, weighted,
and then the value of which is going to be
eu-central-1, in here.
And I'm going to send it as a weighted record.
I'm going to send 20 as weights, and the record ID

And the TTL three seconds.
So now let's go ahead and create these records.

# 288. [SAA/DVA] Route 53 Health Checks
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193858
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about Health Checks
in Route 53.
So health checks are a way for you to check
the health of mainly public resources,
although there's a way for us to do it
for private resources as well, as we'll see in this lecture.
So the idea is that, for example,
we have two Load balancers in different regions
and they're public load balancers, okay?
And behind the scenes,
we have our application running in both of them.
So we're running into a multi-region setup
because we want high availability, and so on,
at the region level.
Then we're going to use Route 53 to create DNS records.
So that's when users access our URL, for example,
mydomain.com, then they get redirected to, for example,
the closest load balancer they have.
So this would be the case with a latency type of record.
But we want to make sure that, if one region is down,
then we don't send our users to that region,
obviously, right?
So to do so,
we're going to create health checks from Route 53.
So we'll create health checks on the one in us-east-1,
and we will create a health check on our instance
in eu-west-1.
Well, with these two health checks,
we're going to be able to associate them
with our Route 53 records.
And the reason we do so is to get automated DNS failover.
So we have three health checks that are possible.
The ones I just showed you, which are the health check
that monitor an endpoint, which is a public endpoint.
So it could be an application, a server,
or another AWS resource.
It could be a health check
that monitors other health checks,
also called a calculated health check,
or it could be a health check
that monitors a CloudWatch Alarm,
which gives you more control and is helpful for private
resources as we'll see in this lecture.
Finally, these health checks have their own metric
and you can view them in CloudWatch metrics as well.
So let's look at how health checks work
with a specific endpoint.
So if we have a health check for eu-west-1, for an ALB,
then the health checkers of AWS
are coming from all around the world.
So it's not just one health checker.
It's about 15 health checkers from all around the world.
And they're all going to send requests
into our public endpoint to wherever routes we set.
And then if it gets 200 OK code back or the code we defined,
then the resource is deemed healthy.
So about 15 global health checkers
will check the endpoint health,
and then you can set a threshold for healthy or unhealthy.
You can set an interval,
so we have two options.
It could be either 30 seconds for regular health checks
or every 10 seconds, which is a higher cost,
which is what's called a fast health check.
It supports many protocols, so HTTP, and HTTPS, and TCP.
And the rule is that if over 18% of the health checkers
say that the endpoint is healthy,
then Route 53 will consider it healthy,
otherwise it's deemed unhealthy.
And you have the ability to choose
which locations you want to use for the health checks.
Now the health checks will only pass if you have the status
2xx or 3xx status code back from the load balancer
and the health check has a cool capability.
So if it is a text-based response,
then the health checkers can check the first 5,120 bytes
of the response to look for some specific texts
in the response itself.
Finally, very important from a network perspective,
if you want for it to work, obviously,
the health checkers must be able to access your
Application Balancer or whatever endpoints you have.
And so therefore you must allow incoming requests
coming from the Route 53 health checkers' IP address range.
And you can find this address range at the URL
in the bottom right of the screen.
Now the second type of health checks we have
are calculated health checks.
And so this is to combine the results
of multiple health checks into a single health check.
And so if you look at Route 53,
with three EC2 instance,
we can create three health checks.
They're all going to be children health check,
and they can all monitor each EC2 instance one by one.
And then we can define a parent health check,
which is going to be defined
on all these child health checks.
And so the conditions to combine all these health checks
could be an OR, an AND, or a NOT.
You can monitor up to 256 child health checks,
and you can specify how many of the health checks
need to pass to make the parent pass.
So the use case for this,
for example, if you want to have
a parent health check to perform maintenance
on your website without causing
all the health checks to fail.
And so how do we monitor the health of a private resource?
So in case you want to monitor something private,
it's going to be difficult because
while all the Route 53 health checkers
live on the public web, they're outside of your VPC,
so they cannot access private endpoints.
So if it's a private VPC or an on-premises resource.
And so the way we can do it, though,
is to create a CloudWatch Metric
and assign a CloudWatch Alarm on it.
And then you can assign the CloudWatch Alarm
into the health checker.
So the idea is that we're going to monitor
the health of our EC2 instance in a private subnet
with a CloudWatch Metric.
And then if the metric is breached,
we're going to create a CloudWatch Alarm on it.
And when the alarm goes into the alarm state,
then the health checker is going to be
automatically unhealthy
and therefore will have created exactly what we want,
which is a health check on a private resource,
which is the most common use case on how to do it.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

---

# 290. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - Failover
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193860
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about routing policies
and this one is going to be for the failover.
So the idea is that we have route 53 in the middle
and we have EC2 instances,
one is going to be our primary EC2 instance,
and the second one is going to be a secondary,
or disaster recovery, EC2 instance.
In this case, what's going to happen is that we're going
to associate our primary record with a health check,
and this is mandatory.
And if the health check it becomes unhealthy,
then route 53 is going to automatically failover
to the second EC2 instance,
and start sending that result back instead.
And of course the secondary EC2 can also be
associated with the health check as well, if we want it to.
But there can only be one primary and one secondary.
Now the client, when it makes DNS requests,
will automatically get the resource that is deemed healthy.
So if our primary is healthy,
then route 53 will answer with a primary record.
But if the health check is unhealthy, automatically,
we will get the response of the second record,
which really helps us do (indistinct) a failover.
So that's it, let's go in the hands-on
to see how we can practice this.
Okay, so now let's leverage these health checks
and create a failover record.
So in my hosted zone, I'm going to create a record,
and this one's going to be called
failover.stephanetheteacher.com,
and it's the A record,
and the first value is going to be
for my EU-central-1 instance, so the one close to me,
and the routing policy is going to be a failover.
So the TTL will set it something really low,
like 60 seconds.
And the failover record type has two options.
It could be either primary or secondary, just these two.
So this is my primary record, and I will associate it
with a health check, I have to.
So it will associate with my health check
named EU-central-1,
and the record ID is going to be E.
So what this is saying is that this record
should be my primary one,
but this is going to be associated with a health check,
which means that you can failover to a second record.
So let's add a new record, and I will keep the record name
as failover.stephanetheteacher.com,
and the value of which is going to be my instance
in US-east-1.
Okay, we're still going to have to do a failover,
the TTL is 60 seconds,
and the failover record type is going to be secondary.

# 292. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - Geoproximity
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/27517998
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about another feature
which is called Geoproximity Routing.
And it can be a little bit confusing
but I will try to explain with diagrams
in the very next slide to make it clear.
So this allows you to route traffic to your resources based
on the geographic location of your users and resources.
So the idea is that with this policy,
you're able using a number called the bias
to shift more traffic to resources
based on specific locations.
And it will show you this in a diagram
in the very next slide.
So the idea is that to change the size
of a geographic location, you need to specify a bias value.
If you want more traffic to go to a specific resource,
you expand the bias value by increasing it.
And if you want less traffic to go to your resource,
you shrink it, you decrease the bias values
to a negative number.
So the resources can be resources from AWS,
in which case you specify the region they're in
and automatically a list will compute the correct routing.
Or if there are none, AWS resources exercise
such as your on premises data center.
Then, you will just need to specify the latitude
and longitude, so the AWS knows where they are right now.
And then it chooses feature,
you need to use the advanced Route 53 Traffic
flow to be able to leverage the bias.
So the diagram should make everything more simple.
And to me, this is what you should remember.
So let's take an example of a resource in us-west-1,
and one resource in us-east-1.
And the bias is set to zero in both regions.
So that means that if you have users all around the US
trying to access these resources,
there's going to be a line dividing the US is too into two,
and users left of that line will go to us-west-1,
and user rights of that line will go to us-east-1.
Now, this is simple, this is when there is no bias, okay?
And this looks like going to the closest resource region
based on the user location.
But thanks to the bias, we can have the same setup
but a different way to have the users routed
to different regions.
So let's take an example.
We have us-west-1 and us-east-1,
and the bias is set to zero in us-west-1,
but we're going to have a positive bias of 50 in us-east-1.
And we've seen that the bias make more users
and more traffic to that resource.
Why?
Well, because of the bias now the quote in quote,
dividing line between the first.
The two resources is going to be a little bit more
to the left because of the higher bias of us-east-1.
And so that means is that's the user left
of that line can go to us-west-1,
but the users right or that one will go to us-east-1.
So what we do this?
Well, for example, you would set your resources
all around the world and say you needed to shift
more traffic to a specific region.
What you would do is that you will use
a Geoproximity Routing Policy to increase the bias
in that specific region.
And therefore, have more users dragged
and more users have traffic attracted to that region.
So what you to remember going into an exam is
that the Geoproximity Routing is really helpful
when you need to shift traffic
from one region to another, by increasing the bias.
Okay?
So hopefully the diagrams helped you make more sense
of the Geoproximity Routing Policy.
I hope you liked this lecture,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 294. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - IP-based
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/37045736
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about another routing policy
called the IP-based Routing
which is very intuitive to think about
because you're going to define the routing based
on the client IP addresses.
In Route 53, you're going to define a list of CIDRs,
they are IP ranges for your clients,
and you're going to say, based on the CIDR
which location the traffic should be sent to.
So the use cases will be to optimize performance
because you know the IP ahead of time
or to reduce network costs
because you know where the IPs are coming from.
So an example is that if you know
that you have a specific internet provider
and they are using a specific CIDR of IP addresses
you can route them
to a specific endpoint thanks to this strategy.
So let's go for an example.
In Route 53, I'm going to define two locations
with two different CIDR blocks.
As you can see, one start with 203
and the other one start with 200 and the defined IP ranges.
Now we are going to link these locations
to a specific record.
So for example.com we're going to have location one.
So the first CIDR block to send
to the value 1.2.3.4,
and the second location, the CIDR block number two,
to send it to 5.6.7.8.
And these represents the public IP of two EC2 instances.
Now, as you would expect, if a user comes in
with a specific IP that is part
of the location one CIDR block, they will be directed
to the first EC2 instance of IP 1.2.3.4,
and the user B, with a second IP address
that belongs to the location two,
will be redirected and will have a DNS query response
to the EC2 instance of IP 5.6.7.8.
And that's it for IP based routing.
It's very simple and I hope you liked it.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 295. [SAA/DVA] Routing Policy - Multi Value
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193870
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Let's talk about the last routing policy,
which is Multi-Value,
which is going to be used when you want to route traffic
to multiple resources.
And Route 53 will therefore
return multiple values or resources.
Now, you can associate them with Health Checks,
and so therefore the only resources returned
via the Multi-Value policy are going to be the ones
that are associated with a healthy Health Check.
So up to eight healthy records are going to be returned
for each Multi-Value query.
And although it looks like an ELB,
it's not a substitute for having an ELB.
The idea is that it's the client-side load balancing.
So let's look at an example.
We are going to set up multiple A Records
for our example.com,
and we associate them with Health Checks.
So when a Multi-Value query is done by our clients,
it's going to receive up to eight records back,
and then the clients will choose one of them.
But at least by combining this with Health Checks,
we know that one of the eight records being returned,
or up to eight, are going to be healthy.
And therefore the client
can have very safe queries into them.
This is going to be different, for example,
when you have a simple routing with multiple values in it,
because as you know, the simple routing policy
does not allow for Health Checks,
and therefore it's possible
that one of the resources returned in the query
of a simple routing policy will be unhealthy.
This is why Multi-Value are a little bit more powerful
as types of records.
So let's have a look in the UI at how we can test them.
So let's practice the Multi-Value record.
So let's go and create a multi-record,
so a multi dot blah blah blah.
And then the value of it
is going to be linked to us-east-1.
So I will add this value here,
and then the Routing policy is going to be Multivalue.
The Health check is going to be us-east-1.
And the Record is going to be US.
And TTL is going to be 60 seconds.
Let's add another Record.
So, multi, and again,
we're going to route to a different region,
so this one is ap-southeast-1.
So the answer is Multivalue answer.
The Health check is ap-southeast-1.
And the Record ID is going to be Asia.
And then the record TTL is one minute.
And then finally, the last one,
so again, one more Record name.
The Value is going to be linked to eu-central-1 right here.
The TTL is one minute.
And the Routing policy is Multivalue answer.
And for the Health checks,
we're going to use the one from eu-central-1.
And the Record ID is EU.
Okay, so let's create these records.
And the records are successfully created.
Now let's test it out.
So for this, we're going to use our CloudShell in here.
So let's reconnect to CloudShell.
And what I want to do is to test this record.
So I will copy the record in here,
and then I will clear my screen.
And so if I test a dig on this,
then I get three answers.
So the three IPs are returned,
and the reason is, well,
the three health checks are fully working.
So as you can see, they're all healthy.
But if I take one of them, for example,
I remove the eu-central-1,
so I'm gonna make this one unhealthy,
and I'm just going to trick it
by editing and do an Invert health status.
So this is going to make the healthy unhealthy,
and vice versa.
It's just a quick way for me
to create an unhealthy health check.
So let me pause right now.
Okay, so now my eu-central-1 health check is Unhealthy.

# 296. [SAA/DVA] 3rd Party Domains & Route 53
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13193874
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we need to make the distinction
between a domain registrar and a DNS service.
So actually you can buy your domain name
with any kind of domain registrar you want,
and you're going to pay annual charges.
So the way we did it so far in this course
was to use the Amazon Registrar,
through the Route 53 console,
but it's possible for you to use any domain name registrar.
So for example, you can use GoDaddy,
you can just Google Domains, and so on.
And usually whenever you register a domain
with a domain registrar,
they will provide you as well with a DNS service
to manage your DNS records.
So when we created a,
when registered a DNS name with a host name with Amazon,
we had a Route 53 hosted zone to manage our DNS records.
But it's possible for you to choose not to use, for example,
AWS Route 53 as your DNS records,
when you have registered your domain with Amazon Registrar.
Or vice versa, you can, for example,
register your domain with GoDaddy.
So you're going to purchase example.com,
yet you're going to use Amazon Route 53
to manage your DNS records.
It's a perfectly acceptable combination.
So how do we do this?
Well, on GoDaddy you're going to register your domain,
and then you're going to have the name servers option,
and you can specify custom name servers.
So what do we put in there?
Well, first we're going to go to Amazon Route 53,
and we're going to create a public hosted zone,
for any domain we want.
And then in the hosted zone details,
we're going to find name servers on the right-hand side.
So these four name servers are the ones
we're are going to have to change on the GoDaddy websites.
So that's when GoDaddy answers a query,
"Hey, which name server should I use?"
the name servers are going to be pointing to
Amazon Route 53 name servers,
and therefore we can use Amazon Route 53
to manage all the EDNS records
that are cleaved from that console.
So to summarize,
if you buy your domain on a third-party registrar,
you can still use Route 53 as your DNS service provider.
For this, you will create a public hosted zone in Route 53,
and then you will update the NS, or name server's records,
on the third-party website, where you bought your domain.
And then you're going to point them
to the Routes 53 name servers.
So, just so you know, a domain registrar looks like,
but is different from a DNS service,
even though every domain registrar
usually comes with some DNS features.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

So a question that can come up is

and you own the domain name exemple.com.

through acme.example.com, with the HTTP protocol.

with the exact same name.
And this is a very, very important
to have the exact same name as the target record.

# 298. Route 53 Resolvers & Hybrid DNS
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/28647158
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so let's have a little talk
about the Route 53 Resolver.
So the idea is that by default,
when you have a Route 53 Resolver,
which is the basic thing you create in Route 53
when you start using it,
it will answer DNS queries
for the local domain names for your EC2 instances
for the records in your private hosted zones,
as well as for the records in your public name server.
So everything you create under Route 53
is going to be answered within your account.
But you may want to have a situation
where you want a hybrid DNS.
That means that you want this resolver to resolve
as well the DNS of your own network and vice versa.
So you want to establish connectivity
between your AWS Cloud DNS
and the DNS of your on-premises network.
And so how do we do this?
For this, we're going to use what's called
a Resolver endpoint.
So this is just a simplified version,
but the idea is that we're going
to create an inbound endpoint
that will allow the DNS resolvers of on-premises resources
to resolve domain names of AWS resources.
So how does that work?
Say we have established
our own Route 53 Resolver in our cloud
and we have an EC2 instance, a private hosted zone,
and we have our on-premises data center.
A server on it is going to be, first of all,
we need to establish of course,
connectivity between our data center and AWS
using a VPN or a direct connect connection.
And then this server is going to do a DNS query,
for example, to look for a domain name
that belongs to our private hosted zone,
is going to be passed to the closest DNS resolver,
so the on-premises resolver,
and these resolver are going to be set up to talk
to a resolver inbound endpoint,
and to pass on this DNS query into our AWS Cloud.
And this resolver knows how to talk
to the Route 53 Resolver.
So this is how you have the full chain
of lookups from your on-premises data center
to your cloud using an inbound endpoint.
And of course you can do it the other way
with an outbound endpoint in which your Route 53 Resolver
will forward DNS queries to your resolver on-premises.
So again, if we have a look,
we have the two infrastructures that are connected,
and then we're going to have a resolver outbound endpoint.
And this time whenever you EC2 instance queries
for a DNS query that is resolved on-premises,
for example, web.onpremise.private,
is going to be passed through the resolver outbound endpoint
to the DNS resolvers of the on-premises data center,
and we'll be good to go.
So that's it.
The idea behind this, I think, a bit complicated lecture
is that if you want to connect
your on-premises data center and AWS
and make sure the DNS queries are resolved both ways,
you must use the resolver inbound and outbound endpoint.
And that's about it. All you should know.
All right, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 299. Route 53 - DNS Query Logging
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53218801
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So for security and logging purposes,
it is possible to log the DNS queries made to Route 53.
So the DNS query logging is going to be a feature
to log information about all the public DNS queries
that your Route 53 Resolver receives.
So this is only applicable to the public hosted zones.
And these can be sent to CloudWatch Logs, for example,
and then from CloudWatch Logs,
you can export them into Amazon S3.
So this is what would happen in your CloudWatch log,
and we have the log format version,
we'll have the timestamp,
we'll have the hosted zone ID that received this query,
the query name, then the query type, the response code,
the protocol, the edge location, the Resolver IP address,
and the EDNS client subnets.
So this is the DNS query logging feature
for public hosted zone,
and they go directly into CloudWatch Logs.
Now, the second kind we have is the Resolver query logging.
So this is to log all DNS queries
made by resources within your VPC.
So we have private hosted zones,
or the Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints,
or the Resolver DNS Firewall.
So a second example,
we have an EC2 instance within a VPC.
It's going to send an example.com query
into your Route 53 Resolver.
Then thanks to the Resolver query logging, okay?
So this is for private resources,
then is going to be sent to either your S3 buckets
or CloudWatch Logs, or even Kinesis Data Firehose.
Remember this?
And then, this configuration can be shared
with other AWS accounts using, again,
the AWS Resource Access Manager service,
or the RAM, AWS RAM service.
What is logged within a Resolver query logging?
Well, this is a JSON document that looks like this,
which again, contains a lot of queries and inserts,
versions, account IDs, and so on, okay?
So let's say for this lecture
now you know the two ways Route 53 can do logging,
either using DNS query logging or Resolver query logging.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 300. Route 53 - Resolver DNS Firewall
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217823
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.
The idea is that you have a managed firewall
that enables you to filter outbound DNS requests
going out through the Route 53 Resolver.
So the idea is that your EC2 instance, for example,
is doing a DNS query to example.com,
the Route 53 Resolver
is going to go through the DNS Firewall,
and if you've configured it properly, to block it,
then it's going to block the request
and come back with no data.
The idea is that now you have control
over attacks, for example.
So say you have a malicious domain
that you don't want to be able to do DNS queries on,
then this is the way to do it.
Or you can whitelist trusted domains.
So here, for example,
we can prevent a compromised application within our VPC
to send data out through DNS to a malicious domain,
an attack called DNS exfiltration.
So all of this can be managed and configured
from the AWS Firewall Manager service.
And all the logs of this Resolver DNS Firewall
can be sent to CloudWatch Logs
and Route 53 Resolver Query Logs.
So it's just a security feature you need to know about,
but an important one at the exam.
All right, that's it. I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 301. Route 53 - Application Recovery Controller
# Section: Networking - Route 53
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217805
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about Route 53
Application Recovery Controller.
So it's a way for you to automate
and orchestrate application recovery
across availability zones and regions.
The idea is that it's a service
meant for mission-critical applications
that need high availability and minimal downtime.
So it's a way for you to manage multi-region active/standby
or active/active setups.
And it's necessary if you have an environment
with regulatory or business continuity requirements.
So how does that work? Well, you have readiness checks.
You're going to check continuously
to validate that the standby
and the replica infrastructure is ready.
And you have routing control and DNS integration.
So you have traffic switches to reroute users
between the different AZs and regions
via DNS and health checks.
You can also do a full zonal shift and region shift
to shift traffic away from impaired AZs
or orchestrate a full region-level failover.
So let me show you in a diagram.
So say you have a region that is active in us-east-1,
you have an application balancer,
EC2 instances across several AZs,
and DynamoDB in the background.
And say you have created a standby region in eu-west-2,
with, again, an ALB and the exact same architecture.
You're going to use Route 53,
you're going to create a recovery group
thanks to Application Recovery Controller.
And then you're going to create resource sets.
So one for your load balancers, one for your EC2 instances,
and one for DynamoDB.
And you're going to have readiness checks within.
And so whenever you're ready, you can fail over,
provided that the readiness checks are okay,
but Route 53 is going to be the overarching service
that's going to make sure that you can perform your failover
and your disaster recovery.
So it's the one service in AWS that can be helpful
for these kind of use cases.
All right, that's it, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

Okay, so now let's talk about CIDR or CIDRs

Well, CIDR has two components.

# 308. [SAA] VPC Overview
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13221966
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's go ahead with creating
our first VPC in AWS.
So VPC stands for Virtual Private Cloud.
And you can have multiple VPC within a single AWS region.
You could have a maximum of five per region,
but this is a soft limit, so you can increase it.
And the number of CIDRs assigned per VPC is five.
Now for each CIDR, the minimum size is /28,
so that means at least 16 IP addresses.
The maximum size is /16, which is at max
65,536 IP addresses.
And because VPC is a private resource,
only Private IPv4 ranges are allowed.
So again, as a reminder, we have this range,
that range, and that range.
Now how do we choose the range for our VPC
in terms of what types of VP are we going to assign to it?
Well, the general rule is that you can assign
whatever you want, but you should make sure
that your VPC CIDR does not overlap
with your other VPCs or other networks
or corporate networks, and the reason we do so
is that if you want to connect them together,
we want to make sure the IP addresses
of one VPC or one CIDR do not overlap
with the range of IP addresses of other networks.
So at the end of this hands-on,
we're just going to have within a region a simple VPC.
So let's get started.

# 310. [SAA] Subnet Overview
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13221968
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so the next step is
to add subnets into our VPC.
So we're going to create two subnets.
One will be a public subnet,
and one will be a private subnet.
Now this is going to be within the one availability zone,
and we'll see what makes a subnet public
or a subnet private.
So let's have a look just first at what subnets are.
So a subnet is going to be, again,
a sub-range of IPv4 addresses within your VPC.
And it turns out that's in this range,
AWS will reserved the five IP addresses in it.
So, the first four IP addresses and the last one is reserved
in each subnet.
These IP addresses are not available for use,
and they cannot be assigned as an IP to an EC2 instance.
So for example,
if you have a CIDR block 10.0.0.0/24,
then you're going to have a few reserved IP addresses.
Such as, well, the first one,
which is network address,
the second one,
so .1, which is reserved AWS for the VPC router,
the .2, which is reserved by AWS for mapping
to Amazon provided DNS,
and this is very important,
.3, which is not used yet,
but is reserved for future use.
And we have .255, which is a network broadcast address.
But because AWS does not support broadcast in a VPC,
this address is reserved and cannot be used, okay?
So as an Exam Tip,
if you need 29 IG IP addresses in a sub-net
for EC2 instances,
then you can not choose a subnet of /27
because this is 32 IP addresses, right, in this /27.
But if you remove the five that are reserved IP addresses,
you're going to get 27 addresses,
which are less than the number 29 that we need.
So we need to choose a subnet size of /26
because this gives us 64 IP addresses in that subnet.
And then if you remove the five reserved IP addresses
with sub-59 IP addresses,
which is greater than the 29 we needed, okay?
So, I will see you in the next lecture
to create our first subnets.

# 312. VPC Troubleshooting
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217745
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So some quick troubleshooting wisdom.
You cannot change or modify the IPv4 CIDR block
of an existing VPC.
You can remove and add a new IPv4 CIDR block instead
or add a secondary IPv4 CIDR block.
Or you can create a new VPC
with a different IPv4 CIDR block.
For example, this would be the case
when your VPC CIDR conflicts with another VPC
or with on-premises CIDR block.
You cannot also change or modify the IPv4 CIDR block
of an existing Subnet.
What you can do is you can create a new Subnet
with a new IPv4 CIDR block.
So for example, this is when you would not have enough
IPv4 addresses in your Subnet.
Then you create a new Subnet
with a larger CIDR block.
So these are common networking questions
that can come up the exam, you should know by then,
but it's good to get a refresher.
All right, that's it.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 313. VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM)
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217751
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
VPC IP Address Manager, or IPAM.
It's a way for you to centrally plan, track,
and monitor your IP address spaces.
It gives you a single source of truth
for all your IP address information.
And this can be done across hundreds of accounts and VPC.
So it's one way for you to manage all the addresses.
So you have a scope, which is a top-level container
that encapsulates all the IP address space that you want.
You have the default public and private scope.
And then you have an IP pool,
which is the collection of IP address ranges, or CIDRs,
that can be divided into sub-pools for regional IP pool.
I'll show you a diagram so you better understand
right now in the next slide.
And you can also monitor your IP addresses
and provide alerts when it detects potential issues,
such as potential overlapping IP addresses.
So the use cases is, number one,
a multi-account way to manage your IP address space
across multiple accounts and make sure they don't overlap,
but also to edit public IP usage,
to identify unused IP addresses,
to monitor CIDR allocation,
and to reclaim unused IP addresses.
So here is the example.
We have, in one account,
the VPC IP Address Manager, or IPAM.
And you create a scope.
And in scope, you create this pool.
And so this is the parent IP pool,
and you're saying, "Okay, all the private IP addresses
with a CIDR 10.0.0.0/8 is what I wanna use
across all my accounts."
And then you have different regions or sub-accounts.
And the first region, Region A, will have a child IP pool
with a different CIDR, so /16.
And so any VPC that falls within this child IP pool is okay.
But if you have a VPC that falls outside of this IP pool,
it's not gonna be okay and it's going to be refused.
And so in Region B, you have a different child IP pool
with a different CIDR that don't overlap,
and so therefore, all the VPCs created within
that Region B will not overlap with the VPCs of Region A.
But you can see how this can scale
to all the regions and hundreds of accounts
to make sure nothing overlaps across all your network
and avoid you some headaches in the future.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 316. [SAA] Bastion Hosts
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13221996
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about bastion hosts
and the idea is that our users
want to access an EC2 instance that is
in a private subnet, but we as users,
we are on our computer on the public internet.
So obviously because our EC2 instance
is in a private subnet
we don't have direct internet access to it.
So the trick, or one trick at least,
is to use a bastion host.
The bastion host is an EC2 instance,
that's named bastion host, okay?
And that EC2 instance is special
because it is in a public subnet.
It has its own security group called
the bastion host security group,
then we also have a security group, of course,
for our EC2 instance in the private subnet.
Now, the idea is that the EC2 instance
in the public subnet, our bastion host,
does have access to the EC2 instance in our private subnet,
well, because everything is in our VPC.
So now to access our EC2 instance in the private subnet,
what we do is that we first connect
through SSH to the bastion host
and then connect from the bastion host,
again with SSH, to the EC2 instance in the private subnet.
And it could be one
but it could be as well, many EC2 instances.

# 322. [SAA] Regional NAT Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/55787785
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's have a quick chat
about regional NAT gateways or RNATs.
So it's a new type of NAT gateway that is highly available
and associated directly with your VPC.
So before, the NAT gateway had to be created
within each public subnets,
but now you just create it at the VPC level,
and then you link it to the Internet gateway.
How?
With the route table.
So you create the NAT gateway, it's in your VPC,
and you tell it that anything that goes to the Internet
should go to your Internet gateway.
The added benefit is
that now you don't need to deploy a NAT gateway per AZ,
automatically, this is shared across all the AZs.
You also don't need to maintain public subnets in your VPC
to host the regional NAT gateway.
So no risk for anyone to create resources
in the public subnet
that you didn't want to use in the first place.
Then, you link your private subnet directly
into your NAT gateway using a route table,
and you're good to go.
Your private subnet instances will have access
to the Internet through this NAT gateway.
And automatically, if you add another AZ,
another private subnet in another AZ,
then it will be detected
and the NAT gateway will scale for you.
So this simplifies solution architecture
by having one central NAT gateway per VPC
instead of creating a NAT gateway instance per AZ.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk
about the VPC Reachability Analyzer.
So it's a really cool feature
because it's a network diagnostics tool
that helps you troubleshoot network connectivity
between two end points in your VPC.
So instead of having to dig through
the network configuration
and understand where the error is happening,
this builds a model of network configuration
between these two end points,
and then it will build and check the reachability
based on the configuration within your AWS accounts.
It doesn't not actually send back it
from source to destination.
It just analyzes your configuration
and tell you what's happening, which is very, very powerful.
So if we take an example of two EC2 instances, okay,
it says A and B.
They may be in different VPCs,
they have different ENIs
and they may have different security groups, okay?
And we're trying to figure out whether or not
Instance A can talk to Instance B.
So there's a bunch of things that need to happen, okay?
So first it goes from the Instance A to the ENI
then to the security group,
then to the network SCLs maybe,
and then to the security group
and through the ENI to Instance B,
and so all along the way,
this Network Reachability Analyzer Tool
from the VPC function is going to check
whether every single point is configured properly.
And in which case it will say, yes,
these two can communicate, they are reachable,
but in case they're not reachable,
for example, because of security group issue,
then it will automatically detect that one security group
will not allow traffic in.
And therefore your Instance B will not be reachable
from Instance A but all of this is done
by just analyzing network configuration,
not by sending packets.
So this is the idea,
and this is why it's super cool,
because he will tell you exactly.
Hey, your route table right here
is just not properly configured.
So the use cases for this is to do a troubleshooting of
connectivity issues and to ensure the network configuration
is made as intended.
So that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it.

# 330. VPC Block Public Access (BPA)
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/53217691
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk
about VPC Block Public Access feature, or BPA.
It's a way for you to centrally block ingress
or egress internet access to VPCs and subnets.
What does that mean?
It means traffic that goes from the internet
into your account
or traffic that goes from your account to the internet.
So, why would you wanna do this?
Well, it helps you ensure compliance
and security requirements.
So you have two modes.
Bidirectional, in which you block all internet traffic
to and from the VPCs to ensure that no matter what,
you will never touch the internet.
Or ingress-only to block all traffic to or from the VPCs,
except for NAT gateways and egress-only internet gateways.
That means that the instances within your accounts
will be able to communicate with the internet, for example,
to pull updates or data,
but the internet will never be able to access
whatever is in your account.
Then, you also have the ability
to include single VPCs and subnets with two exclusion modes.
You have bidirectional to allow all internet traffic
to or from the excluded VPCs and subnets,
or egress-only to only allow outbound internet
from the excluded VPCs and subnets.
So it's just an exclusion mode on the two modes from before.
This can be enabled for each AWS Region
and you can verify if the traffic is blocked
using, for example, the VPC Reachability Analyzer tool.
So it's a great way for you to have a rule above all of them
to make sure you block public access
and you are very secure.
All right, that's it, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 331. [SAA] VPC Peering
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13221988
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about VPC Peering.
So the idea is that we can create VPCs
and in different regions, different accounts
and we want to connect them together using the AWS network.
Why we do this?
Well, we wanna make them behave
as if they were in the same network, okay?
So it could be very specific.
Maybe you could have VPC in other regions
in other accounts, or even within your same accounts
and you want to connect them.
So in order for them not to connect, remember, I said,
the VPC network CIDRs must be distant from each other
because when we connect them together,
if they have overlapping CIDRs,
they will not be able to communicate.
So, VPC peerings can happen between two VPCs
and they're not transitive.
That means that each VPC
that wants to communicate with one another
must have VPC peering enabled.
So if you have a look at three VPCs right now, A, B, and C,
then we can create a peering connection between A and B.
And this is allowing you to connect them together.
And we can create another peering connection
between VPC B and C,
and again, they can communicate together.
But even though A and B, and B and C, are connected,
you still need to enable a VPC peering connection
between A and C, to have them communicate.
This is very, very, very, very important.
Finally, even though your VPC are peered with each other,
you must also make sure that you update all the route tables
in each VPC's subnets, to ensure that these two instances
in different VPC, can communicate with each other.
And we'll see this in the hands-on.
So some good things to know about VPC peering.
They can happen within your own accounts,
but they can happen across accounts.
So if you want to connect a VPC from one account A,
to account B, you could, and also across regions.
So this is very, very powerful.
And you remember, in security groups,
we can reference other security groups in it.
While it's possible to also reference a security group
from a peered VPC across accounts in the same region.
And this is very powerful
because we don't need to have the source
as a CIDR on IP, we can also reference a security group.
Extremely powerful.
So back into our networking diagram.
We're here and now we're going to add
a VPC peering connection
to connect our VPC to other VPCs.
So that's it. I will see you in the next lecture.

# 333. [SAA] VPC Endpoints
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13221990
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about VPC endpoints.
The idea is that you have services on AWS, for example,
such as DynamoDB and they are accessible publicly.
So that means that your whole infrastructure
through your NAT gateway and then your internet gateway
or just directly
through your internet gateway does access DynamoDB.
But all this traffic goes through the public internet
and you may have other services such as CloudWatch
and Amazon S3 that you also wanna access
without going through the internet.
You wanna access them privately.
So the idea is that you're going to use VPC endpoints
so that your instances don't have to go
through the public internet,
they can just go directly
through the private AWS network to these services.
So let's consider this architecture that we know already,
so we have public subnets with a NAT gateway
and it's EC2 instance, a private subnet,
and then we're going to have an internet gateway
so that we know we can access the Amazon SNS service
for example, through different ways.
So if we look at the private subnet
and the EC2 instance in it,
to access the Amazon SNS service,
the EC2 instance can go through the NAT gateway
which then goes to the internet gateway
and then accesses publicly the Amazon SNS service
and this is the same
for the EC2 instance in the public subnet,
it goes directly through the internet gateway
to the Amazon SNS service.
And this option is fine
but it costs just a lot of money because, well,
we have to go through NAT gateway, which has a cost,
and then we have to go through the internet gateway
which doesn't have a cost
but still there is obviously many hops
and it's not very efficient.
So instead, I'm just representing
the same Amazon SNS service,
but somewhere else on the diagram,
we can use a VPC endpoint.
And the idea is that the VPC endpoint is deployed
within your VPC and by doing some networking,
we can actually make the EC2 instance
in the private subnet go through the VPC endpoint
directly into the Amazon SNS service
and the network has never left AWS, which is really good.
So, every AWS service is publicly exposed,
it has public a URL,
and if you use VPC endpoints, they are powered
by something called AWS PrivateLink because you
access these services privately.
Then you can connect to any of these services
by AWS using a private network
instead of going over the public internet.
These VPC endpoints are redundant and they scale
horizontally, and they're going to remove the need
for an internet gateway or a NAT gateway
to access AWS services,
thus simplifying your network infrastructure by a lot.
So in case of issues, you need to check the DNS
settings resolution in your VPC and your route tables.
So this is the general idea behind the VPC endpoints now,
we have two types of VPC endpoints.
We have the Interface Endpoints
and these are powered by PrivateLink
and we have the Gateway Endpoints.
So the Interface Endpoints provision an ENI,
so it's a private IP address in your VPC
and this ENI is an entry point to your private AWS service.
And so for this, we must attach a security group
because there is an ENI and it supports most AWS services
if not all, and there's a cost to it, it's a cost
per hour and it's a cost per gigabyte of data processed.
So here we go, we have an EC2 instance
and a private subnet and thanks to a PrivateLink
VPC endpoint of type interface
then we can access through the ENI to the service.
And this works for every single service out there.
Now we have the Gateway Endpoint and they're special.
They provision what's called a gateway
and this has to be used as a target in a route table.
So this does not leverage IP addresses,
this is not a leverage security groups,
it's just a target in a route table
and you need to remember that.
And there are only two targets for a Gateway Endpoint,
it is Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, but the advantage
that this is free and this scales automatically
because it's only a route table access.
So, it's only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, remember this.
And in this instance,
we provide a VPC endpoint of type gateway
and we have access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB.
So the question you may ask me is, hey,
if the Interface Endpoint supports everything
and the Gateway Endpoint supports Amazon S3 and DynamoDB,
should I use the Gateway
or the Interface Endpoint for Amazon S3 or DynamoDB?
Well, we have indeed two ways
of accessing Amazon S3, right?
Either with the Gateway Endpoint
or with an Interface Endpoint.
And at the exam, the Gateway is most likely going to
be the preferred solution at the exam, why?
Well, because we just have to modify a route table.
So, and your apps can access Amazon S3 free of charge,
so the cost is free for a Gateway, it scales more,
and for the Interface Endpoint,
you have a cost associated with it.
The only time where an Interface Endpoint may be preferable
over a Gateway Endpoint is
if you require access from on-premises, for example
you want private access from your on-premise data center
and we haven't seen it yet, but we can connect it
through something called site to site VPN or direct connect
or it's maybe preferable if you want to connect
from another VPC through this Interface Endpoint.
So these are advanced use cases, right?
And this is what is represented on this graph.
But most of the time
the Gateway Endpoint is going to be preferred
for Amazon S3.
Okay, that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 335. [SAA] VPC Flow Logs
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/28876036
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about VPC Flow Logs.
VPP flow logs allow you
to capture information from IP traffic going
into your interfaces.
So that could be at the VPC level, the subnet level,
or the elastic network interface, ENI level.
So we have three kinds of flow logs.
They're very helpful to monitor
and troubleshoot connectivity issues
happening within your VPC.
So these flow logs can be sent to Amazon S3,
CloudWatch Logs, and Kinesis Data Firehose,
and they will capture information
for also AWS managed interfaces such as ELB, RDS,
ElasticCache, Redshift, Workspaces, your net gateway,
your transit gateway, and so on.
So this is what a VPC flow log looks like.
So there is a format associated with it,
but there is a version, account ID, interface ID,
source address, destination address,
source port, destination port, protocol packets by start
and action and log status.
So this is metadata about the network packets
going into your VPC.
And you don't need to remember this at a high-level, right?
But let's have a look at
what information we can get out of these flow logs.
So the source address and the destination address
help identify problematic IP.
This is where you see if an IP is repeatedly being denied,
maybe there is something wrong with that IP,
or maybe you're being attacked by a specific IP, source port
and destination port helps you identify the probiotic ports.
Action is going to be either accept or reject.
And so it's going to say whether or not it's a success
or failure at the SG or NACL level.
And we'll see this in the very next slide.
And so this can be used the VPC logs
to do analytics on usage patterns
or detect manage behavior, port scans, and so on.
Now, to query these flow logs,
you have two ways of doing it.
The best way is to do Athena on S3,
or if you wanted to do a streaming analysis,
you could use CloudWatch logs insights.
So here are some examples
that you can have a look on your own time for flow logs.
So how do we use flow logs to troubleshoot security group
and NACL issues?
Well, we look at the action field.
So let's have a look at the typical incoming request
for your NACL and your subnet.
So remember, your NACL are stateless
and your security groups are stateful.
So what happens?
Well, if we get an inbound reject,
so we see that the inbound request from from the outside
to our EC2 instance is rejected.
That can means that either from this graph,
the NACL is refusing the request
or the security group is refusing the request.
And this makes sense, right?
But if we have a inbound accept
and an outbound reject, it can only mean a NACL issue.
Why?
Or because your security group is stateful.
And if the inbound is allowed
because of the accept, automatically the outbound
will be allowed thanks to the statefulness
of your security group.
So for outgoing request, similar analysis, right?
This is the diagram we know already.
And so if you get an outbound reject,
then you have a NACL or a security group issue.
But if you get an outbound accept and inbound reject,
then it must mean a NACL issue.
So let's have a look at a few architectures
for your VPC flow logs

# 337. [SAA] Site to Site VPN, Virtual Private Gateway & Customer Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-cloudops-associate/learn/lecture/13222006
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk
about site-to-site VPN.
So the idea is that, now we have a VPC
but we may have also a structure
within the corporate data center,
and we wanna connect AWS to our corporate data center
using a private connection.
So for this, we'll have a customer gateway
on the corporation side,
and a VPN gateway on the VPC side.
And we're going to establish,
through the public internet,
a private site-to-site VPN connection.
So it's a VPN connection, so it's encrypted.
It goes over the public internet, though.
And using this, we have linked effectively
the network of our VBC
to the network of our corporate data center.
So, as such, the VPNs need two things.
First, they need a virtual private gateway, VGW.
It's a VPN concentrator on the AWS side
of the VPN connection,
and the VGW is created and attached to the VPC
from which you want to create
the site-to-site VPN connection.
It's possible for you to customize the ASN number,
if you know what that means.
The customer gateway is a CGW,
and it's an actual software
or a physical device on your side,
so on the data center side of the VPN connection,
And there's a bunch of these
that will have been tested by AWS,
so we can have a look at the list here.
So, to do a connection, it's very simple.
We have a corporate data center with a customer gateway,
and then we have our VPC with our virtual private gateway.
So, how do we set up the customer gateway device
that is on premises?
Which IP address should we use?
Well, if your customer gateway is public,
there is a public internet-routable IP address
for your customer gateway device.
Then you would use this one,
and you would establish the connectivity
between your VGW and your CGW
using the public IP of the customer gateway.
But it's possible for your customer gateway
to also be private and have a private IP.
In which case, then it is very common for it
to be behind a NAT device that has NAT-T enabled.
And then, that NAT device has a public IP, in which case,
the IP address you should use for the CGW
is the public IP of the NAT device.
And then, the site-to-site VPN connection
can be established.
I'm saying this because this can come into the exam.
And then, the second question that can come up
to the exam is that,
even though this is set up,
this site-to-site VPN connection will not work
until you enable route propagation in your VPC
within your subnets.
And then, when this is done,
then the connectivity will work.
Finally, another exam question that can come up
regarding site-to-site VPN.
If you need to ping your EC2 instances
from on-premises to AWS,
then make sure that the ICMP protocol on the inbound
of the security group is enabled.
Otherwise, I would say the connection will not work.
This is just a security group question, obviously.
But they mix it up with the site-to-site VPN
and that can be confusing, so here is some help.
Now, there's one last thing to know
about a site-to-site VPN.
It's called AWS VPN CloudHub.
So the idea is that you have your VPC with your VGW
and you have multiple customer networks,
multiple data centers, each with their own customer gateway.
So CloudHub is to provide secure communication
in between all these sites, using multiple VPN connections.
It's a low-cost hub-and-spoke model
for primary or secondary network connectivity
between different locations,
but only using the VPN.
So you would establish a site-to-site VPN
between the CGW and the one single VGW within your VPC.
And then, thanks to this connection,
then your customer networks can now communicate
with one another through that VPN connection.
Now, because it's a VPN connection,
all the traffic goes over the public internet.
So they're not connected through a private network.
They're connected through public network
but the VPN connection is encrypted, obviously.
And to set it up, super simple,
you set up multiple site-to-site VPN connection
on the same virtual private gateway,
and then you enable dynamic routing
and you configure your route tables, and you're good to go.
So that's it.
That's all you need to know for site-to-site VPN.
